commentary.historical_context: The deployment of three thousand soldiers to hunt one man in the wilderness represents a significant military mobilization. In the ancient Near East, such forces would typically be mobilized to counter external invasion or suppress rebellion. The fact that Saul can marshal this force shows Israel's military development under his kingship, yet it also reveals the instability of his reign: he must constantly validate his authority by pursuing the man the people favor. The 'rocks of the wild goats' are the Judean limestone cliffs, one of the oldest known inhabited human regions on earth. Archaeological surveys show these cliffs riddled with caves; many would be invisible from below and accessible only by rope or intimate knowledge of the terrain. Saul's foot soldiers, marching in formation and encumbered with supplies and armor, would be exhausted and exposed in such terrain.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 17-19, King Noah pursues Abinadi, who 'fled out of the city' into the wilderness. Like Saul, Noah represents corrupt political power using state machinery to suppress the righteous. The comparison highlights how persecutions are often personal vendetta dressed in official authority.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 addresses persecution: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversaries shall be confounded.' David's situation—hunted by a jealous king—parallels the experiences of Joseph Smith and early Saints. The principle is that the Lord's anointed are given refuge even when pursued by overwhelming force.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the 'rock' and 'stronghold' that Saul's power cannot penetrate. Covenant ordinances create a spiritual topography that nullifies the enemy's numerical advantage, much as the cliffs of En-gedi nullify Saul's military superiority.

commentary.christological_typology: Saul's relentless pursuit of David with overwhelming force prefigures the powers of darkness pursuing Christ. Yet terrain and numbers cannot determine outcomes when God ordains otherwise. As David will escape Saul's grasp despite the numerical disadvantage, Christ's resurrection will overturn the apparent victory of those who sought his death.
commentary.application: When we find ourselves in conflict with those wielding institutional power—whether in workplace, family, or social settings—we must remember that numerical superiority and official authority do not determine God's purposes. Our task is not to match our enemy's force but to position ourselves on the 'terrain' where faith is strongest: in prayer, in community with the covenant faithful, in the scriptures, in the temple. Like David at En-gedi, we should seek the high ground of moral clarity and spiritual preparation rather than engage in direct combat where we cannot win. Saul's 'three thousand men' are ultimately powerless against a man who trusts in the God of Israel.

text_kjv: And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave.

commentary.narrative: This verse contains the narrative setup for the central moral crisis of the chapter. Saul, while searching for David among the cliffs, discovers a cave near some sheep pens and enters it. The Hebrew phrase lehasekh et raglav ('to cover his feet') is a well-known biblical euphemism for defecation—the reference is anatomical and deliberate. Saul, the king of Israel, enters the cave for the purpose of relieving himself. Meanwhile, David and his men are already there, sitting 'deep in the recesses of the cave' (beyarketei hamme'arah). The noun yarketei, which The Covenant Rendering employs, means the innermost or remotest parts—the same word used for the far reaches of a ship in Jonah 1:5 or the remote reaches of the north in Isaiah 14:13. The cave is deep enough, and Saul's eyes are adjusted to the brightness of the midday desert, that he cannot see into the darkness where David and his men sit, watching him. The sheep pens explain the cave's existence: in the ancient Near East, shepherds used natural limestone caves as overnight shelter for flocks. David's band, familiar with the region, would have known these caves intimately. The narrative creates a moment of extreme physical proximity between hunter and hunted, with the hunter completely unaware that his prey is mere feet away, in the darkness behind him, watching his vulnerability.

word_study.meaning: A euphemistic expression. Hasekh means to cover or hide; raglav means 'his feet.' The phrase covers (pun intended) the act of defecation or urination. It derives from the practical reality that when a person squats to relieve themselves, their garments drape down, covering their feet and lower body.
word_study.significance: The TCR translator notes explain that translating this euphemism as 'to relieve himself' is more transparent to modern readers than 'to cover his feet,' which has become impenetrably opaque in modern English. Yet the euphemism itself is narratively significant: the text is emphasizing Saul's vulnerability and loss of royal dignity. The king is stripped of his authority and presence—he is at his most exposed, his most human, his most undignified. This is not crude humor; it is narrative strategy. The reader is being positioned to feel the vulnerability that makes the coming action both possible and weighty.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the innermost parts of the cave.' Yarketei is the plural of yarke, meaning remotest part, far side, or rear. It appears in Psalm 48:2 ('the sides of the north') and Isaiah 14:13 ('the sides of the north'). In spatial contexts, it denotes the far, hidden, deep reaches of a place.
word_study.significance: David and his men are not lurking near the entrance; they are sitting deep inside the cave, hidden in its far recesses. This means they have been living there—not just hiding, but encamped. The verb 'remained' or 'sitting' (yoshvim) is a participle suggesting ongoing habitation. The cave was their base of operations.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'enclosures of the flock' or 'sheep pens.' Gider is a fence or enclosure; tso'n is a flock of sheep. These were practical structures where shepherds could secure their flocks overnight against predators.
word_study.significance: The sheep pens establish the cave's function in the local economy: it was a known shelter used by shepherds. This detail grounds David's presence at En-gedi in practical reality—his men were not simply hiding in a random cave, but occupying a facility known to locals, used seasonally by shepherds who brought their flocks there.

cross_references.connection: These verses immediately follow and show David's decisive moral response to the vulnerability Saul is experiencing at this moment.
The same word 'recesses' (yarketei) describes the 'innermost parts' of the ship where Jonah fled from God's presence—both passages use isolation as a refuge, though with opposite moral trajectories.
Later, when David is fleeing from Absalom, he will encounter Ziba with supplies, demonstrating that his presence in the wilderness was known and supported by elements of the population.

This psalm is attributed to David 'when he was in the cave,' likely referring to this moment: 'Hear my cry...in the cave where I am hiding.' The psalm expresses the emotional reality of hunted innocence.
Jonathan had warned David that 'Saul sought to kill him,' setting up the recurring pattern of David fleeing and seeking refuge in caves and wilderness strongholds.

commentary.historical_context: En-gedi's cave systems are among the most extensively studied in the Levant. Modern surveys have identified dozens of caves, many large enough to shelter dozens of people, some large enough for hundreds. The caves are distributed throughout the cliffs rather than centralized, allowing a distributed defensive posture. The limestone is soft enough that wind and water erosion created natural chambers without requiring significant human excavation. The sheep pen detail is archaeologically significant: shepherds in the ancient Near East regularly used such caves as seasonal enclosures for flocks, particularly during lambing season (spring) and through summer grazing. The caves provided protection from predators (leopards, hyenas, and wild dogs inhabited the region) and from extreme heat during midday. A person entering such a cave from bright desert sunlight would require several minutes for their eyes to adjust to the darkness—a detail that explains how Saul could enter without seeing David's men positioned deep within. The cave mouth was typically darkened by the sheep pen's pens and structures, further reducing visibility from the entrance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:3, Ammon and his companions rejoice in their escape from the Lamanite king: 'We have been cast out, and have wandered in the wilderness even unto this time.' Like David at En-gedi, they are refugees in geographical isolation, relying on the Lord and on their knowledge of terrain to survive.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:50-53 speaks of those who 'received not the testimony of Jesus' dwelling in outer darkness—a kind of spiritual cave from which they cannot see. David's men, hidden in the physical cave but seeing Saul clearly, are a reverse image: they are in darkness but spiritually seeing, while Saul is in the light but spiritually blind.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of sitting deep within a hidden sanctuary, unseen by enemies but present and watching, resonates with the temple endowment: the initiate moves through increasingly protected spaces, ultimately seated in the celestial room, hidden from the world's opposition yet present in God's house.

commentary.christological_typology: This scene prefigures Christ in the tomb—hidden in the earth, unseen by those who thought they had defeated him, yet present and alive, about to work a salvation that those outside the tomb cannot foresee. The cave becomes a type of the sepulcher, and David's men, watching, become types of the faithful remnant awaiting resurrection.
commentary.application: The moment of Saul's vulnerability—his exposure in the cave—represents the principle that our enemies' apparent strength often masks profound weakness. When we are aware of this truth, we gain moral clarity. We can see our adversary's situation with clarity while remaining hidden in the Lord's strongholds. But this knowledge brings responsibility: seeing vulnerability in an enemy who is nonetheless God's anointed (or in any person, regardless of their opposition to us) should stir our conscience and constrain our actions. The cave's darkness should not become the hiding place for vengeance, but rather a place where we sit in silence and gain the patience that God requires of us.

text_kjv: And it came to pass afterward, that David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt.

commentary.narrative: After cutting the corner of Saul's robe (described in verse 5, but referenced here in the narrative flow), David's conscience responds with remarkable force. The phrase vayyakh lev David oto ('David's heart struck him') uses the verb nakhah, the same word employed for striking an enemy in battle, for wielding a sword, for smiting with violence. The narrator does not describe David's conscience as whispering or quietly troubling him—it 'struck' him, dealt a blow, assaulted him from within. This language is violent and intentional. David is being struck by his own moral faculty, much as a warrior is struck by an opponent's sword. The cause is explicitly stated: 'because he had cut off Saul's skirt'—the corner (kenaf) of Saul's outer garment. Why did this small act trouble David so profoundly? The answer lies in the layers of meaning embedded in the garment's significance. To cut the corner of the king's robe was to symbolically breach the king's person, to claim authority over the anointed. Even though David's act was secret and cost Saul nothing—Saul did not even know it happened—David's covenant-trained conscience recognized that he had trespassed against the Lord's anointed. He had done what only the Lord has authority to do: to strip away the symbol of kingly authority. In verse 6, David will be even more explicit about why this troubles him: he speaks of 'the Lord's anointed' and refuses to raise his hand against Saul despite having the power and opportunity to do so. David's moral framework is not based on circumstance or opportunity, but on covenant principle.

word_study.term_original: וַיַּ֤ךְ לֵב־דָּוִד֙ אֹת֔וֹ (vayyakh lev David oto)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'his heart struck him.' The verb nakhah means to strike, smite, hit, kill. It is used for military action (striking in battle), for divine judgment (God striking down enemies), and for violence. The subject here is lev (heart) — David's own heart is striking him.
word_study.significance: This is the most violent metaphor the text could employ for conscience. David's conscience is not a soft inner voice; it is a weapon. The same verb that describes warriors striking each other describes David's own moral nature striking him from within. This language reveals that David's conscience is trained, disciplined, and powerful—not a whisper but a warrior. Later, David will 'strike' (nakhah) enemies with the sword in 2 Samuel; here, the only enemy he strikes is himself.

word_study.meaning: Corner, edge, or wing. Derived from the root meaning wing. In garment contexts, kenaf refers to the corner or hem of the outer robe (the me'il), particularly the corner that bore tassels (tsitsit) as commanded in Numbers 15:38. The word is often translated 'skirt' (KJV) but more precisely means the corner or wing of the garment.
word_study.significance: The kenaf was not merely decorative; it was symbolic. In Numbers 15:39, the tsitsit (fringes) attached to the kenaf served as a reminder of covenant commandments. To cut the kenaf was to sever the symbol of that covenant obligation. Moreover, the kenaf's dual meaning—both wing and garment corner—creates theological resonance throughout scripture. Ruth 3:9 uses 'spread your wing (kenaf) over me' to mean protective covering; Psalm 91:4 speaks of being hidden under God's 'wings' (kanaf). To cut Saul's kenaf was, symbolically, to claim or sever the protective authority that belongs only to the anointed king or to the Lord himself.

cross_references.connection: Samuel tore Saul's robe (me'il) as a sign that God was tearing the kingdom from Saul. David's cutting of Saul's kenaf echoes this act, and David's horror may stem from recognizing that he is acting out a divine prerogative.

The scene will repeat: David will have opportunity to kill Saul while he sleeps, and again David will refuse, saying 'The Lord forbid that I should... put forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed.'
The tsitsit (fringes) on the garment's corners were commanded as reminders of covenant. To cut the corner was to remove or symbolically desecrate the covenant reminder attached to it.
Ruth asks Boaz to 'spread your wing (kenaf) over me,' using the same word to request protective covenant covering. Cutting Saul's kenaf removes or threatens this protective covering.

David later condemns the Amalekite who boasts of killing Saul: 'How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the Lord's anointed?' David will demonstrate his principle consistently: the Lord's anointed is inviolable.

commentary.historical_context: The me'il (outer robe) worn by Saul was the garment of authority—the uniform of kingship. In ancient Near Eastern royal contexts, damage to the king's garments carried symbolic and often legal consequences. The corner (kenaf) of such a garment was typically where identifying tassels, embroidery, or markers of rank were affixed. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian contexts, tearing a ruler's garment was sometimes an act of rebellion or insult with serious legal consequences. The Hebrew principle that the garment represents the person ('as a man thinks in his heart, so is he') extended to viewing the king's garments as extensions of his authority and person. Samuel's tearing of Saul's robe in 1 Samuel 15 was understood as a prophetic sign-act, symbolizing God's tearing away of the kingdom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:7, Alma experiences spiritual anguish when his conscience 'began to smite me' (same verb used in 1 Samuel 24:5, translated here as 'struck'). Alma's heart is struck by his guilt over his sins, just as David's is struck by his transgression against the anointed. Both men respond by turning to God for salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45 speaks of the Spirit's 'constant companionship' leading to a 'conscience void of offense toward God and toward all men.' David's struck heart is his conscience exercising exactly this principle: he is offended in himself by what he has done, regardless of external consequences.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes language about being 'clothed' with the robes of the priesthood and with authority. To cut Saul's kenaf is to tamper with sacred vestments; David's horror reflects the temple principle that garments of authority are not to be handled lightly or by those who have no right to them.

commentary.christological_typology: David's internal strike of conscience mirrors the principle of Christ bearing our sins—an inward blow on behalf of wrongdoing. Yet whereas David's conscience condemns him for a small act, Christ becomes the atonement for all humanity's transgressions. David's smiting heart becomes a type of the suffering required for true righteousness.
commentary.application: David's response teaches a crucial principle for covenant life: our conscience should be more powerful, more immediately responsive, more violent in its moral correction than any external pressure. An action that no one else knows about, that causes no external harm, that comes from an opportunity handed to us by providence—such an action becomes the subject of intense internal conflict if we have trained our conscience properly. For modern disciples, this means developing a conscience so attuned to principle that it recoils from even small ethical transgressions. We should cultivate a heart that 'smites' us when we cut corners—whether literal corners (of others' rights, respect, or property) or figurative ones (compromises with principle, rationalizations of sin, or small treacheries). David's conscience is his most powerful weapon, more effective than the sword he carries.

text_kjv: And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the LORD said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul's robe privily.

commentary.narrative: David's men seize the moment. They recognize Saul's vulnerability and immediately invoke divine promise. The Hebrew phrase 'Behold the day' (hinneh hayom) suggests a significant moment—'this is it, this is the day.' They then cite what appears to be a prophecy: 'Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand.' The text does not tell us where or when the Lord made this promise to David, but it would fit with Samuel's anointing of David (16:12-13) and the various occasions where the Spirit of the Lord has confirmed David's future kingship. David's men are arguing that the promise is now being fulfilled—Saul has literally been placed into David's hand, vulnerability displayed, escape route nonexistent. Their logic is compelling from a worldly perspective: opportunity plus promise plus power equals action. Yet David's subsequent actions reveal a different interpretation of what the promise means. David does arise (vayyaqom David), and he does move toward Saul, but what he does is cut off 'the corner of Saul's robe privily' (ballat—stealthily, secretly). The action is restrained compared to what his men have implied he should do. He takes a piece of the royal garment as evidence that he had access to Saul's person, proving that he could have killed him if he had chosen to do so. But taking the garment corner is radically different from taking Saul's life. It is a proof of concept, not an execution. The fact that David does this 'privily' (ballat) suggests his own discomfort with the act; even this limited action is performed in stealth, acknowledging some inner conflict even before his conscience fully responds.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'behold the day.' Hinneh is an exclamation of attention ('look, behold, here'); yom means day. Together, the phrase points to a significant moment—'this is the day, this moment,' often used to mark a pivotal or expected occasion.
word_study.significance: The phrase's use here is ironically charged. David's men are claiming to recognize the fulfillment of prophecy in real time. They believe this is the divinely appointed moment. Yet the text will reveal that they have misunderstood the promise. God's promise to deliver enemies into David's hand does not mean every vulnerable moment is the moment to kill.

word_study.meaning: To give, deliver, place, put. A common verb with many applications. In the phrase 'I am giving your enemy into your hand,' natan describes God placing the enemy within David's power—a literal and a figurative yielding of control.
word_study.significance: The verb encompasses both the giving of power and the giving of the person. David's men interpret this as permission to act. But David will understand the gift differently: he is given power over Saul's life not as permission to take it, but as a test of his character—to prove that he will not.

word_study.meaning: Secretly, stealthily, silently, in stealth. The adverb modifies David's action—he cuts the robe 'in stealth,' without being seen or heard. The word appears rarely (also Ruth 3:7), suggesting covert action.
word_study.significance: David's choice to act 'privily' (ballat) reveals his own internal conflict. He has not yet consciously recognized that cutting the robe is wrong, yet his body moves in stealth—his unconscious wisdom knows that what he is doing requires secrecy. The stealth prefigures his later recoil: an action done in darkness is often an action the heart later rejects.

cross_references.connection: Samuel anoints David as the future king, promising that the Spirit of the Lord will be upon him. This anointing forms the basis of David's men's claim that God has promised to deliver Saul into David's hand.

Earlier, David acknowledges that 'the Lord delivered him into my hand' when referring to Keilah, but he did not harm Saul then either, recognizing the principle that covenant obligation supersedes opportunity.
The scene repeats: Abishai will say 'God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day,' and David will respond, 'the Lord forbid that I should put forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed.'

Later wisdom literature would affirm that 'he that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.' David demonstrates this principle by restraining himself in the moment of greatest power.
David will later execute an Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul, showing that David's refusal to harm the anointed is not situational ethics but principle.

commentary.historical_context: The scene reflects the political reality of ancient Near Eastern kingship: vulnerability of the king, even when surrounded by guards and authority, was a constant concern. Many ancient Near Eastern texts document coups, assassinations, and usurpations by ambitious princes or generals. David's men are thinking in practical political terms—eliminate the threat, secure the kingdom, ensure David's dynasty. Yet David's covenant training pulls him in a different direction. The cutting of the robe's corner would be recognized by anyone familiar with garment symbolism as evidence of proximity and power—'I could have done more but did not.' It serves as a proof of restraint, a public demonstration (once revealed) that David had access and did not act.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:24, Alma teaches his son that the Lord 'will make all things manifest unto thee' if he seeks to follow righteousness. Like David, Alma receives revelation directing him away from killing (his persecutors) and toward serving (his salvation). The principle is that covenanted servants receive guidance that supersedes external circumstances.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-10 speaks of the Lord's servants receiving 'the testimony of Jesus,' which trains them in moral discernment. David's men reason from circumstance; David reasons from covenant. This mirrors the distinction between the carnal mind and the spiritual mind outlined in D&C 67:10.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires the initiate to covenant to obey the law of the Lord and to 'sustain the presiding high priesthood.' Saul, despite his failings, is still the Lord's anointed and therefore the covenant person. David's restraint becomes an expression of temple covenant loyalty to priesthood authority, even when that authority is unworthy.

commentary.christological_typology: David's restraint, despite having power to strike, prefigures Christ's refusal to call down legions of angels to save himself (Matthew 26:53). Both figures have power available to them and refuse to use it, recognizing that moral principle and covenant obligation supersede self-preservation.
commentary.application: David's men represent the voice of practical reasoning—'You have the power, you have the opportunity, you have the promise; therefore act.' This voice is seductive and appears throughout life: in professional conflicts ('You could destroy your rival's credibility and no one would know'), in financial dealings ('This loophole is legal'), in personal relationships ('You're right, they're wrong; you have every right to retaliate'). The wisdom David demonstrates is the ability to hear the practical argument, acknowledge its logic, and then choose a higher principle. He does act (cutting the robe), showing this is not passivity or cowardice, but he acts in restraint, with stealth, in a way that bothers his conscience. This teaches us that sometimes the right response is neither to fully comply with our enemies' logic nor to passively accept injustice, but to take limited, principled action that preserves our covenant integrity. We should develop antennae for the moment when we act 'privily,' in stealth—such moments often signal that our conscience knows something our reasoning has not yet acknowledged.

text_kjv: And it came to pass afterward, that David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt.

commentary.narrative: Immediately after cutting the robe's corner, David's internal reckoning begins. The phrase 'it came to pass afterward' (vayhî achar ken) suggests a moment following the act—the action has been completed, but its moral weight now descends upon David. His heart 'smote him' (vayyakh lev David oto)—the same violent metaphor introduced earlier, now clarified: David's conscience delivers a blow to David's moral self. The word 'struck' (nakhah) is not hyperbolic; it is the text's way of describing moral horror. David has cut a piece of cloth, an act that cost Saul nothing—Saul did not know it happened, was not harmed by it, did not even miss his garment. Yet David's conscience responds as if he has committed a grave sin. Why? The answer lies in what David will articulate in the verses that follow: he has touched the garment of 'the Lord's anointed.' The TCR translator notes highlight a crucial detail: David's act echoes the tearing of Samuel's robe in 1 Samuel 15:27-28, where Samuel tore Saul's robe as a sign-act indicating God was tearing the kingdom from Saul. David has instinctively recognized that by cutting Saul's garment, he was acting out a divine prerogative—he was claiming authority that belongs only to God. Saul is God's anointed. Even to symbolically strip him of authority, even in secret, even with no harm done, is to trespass against the Lord's own agent. David's covenant-trained conscience recognizes this immediately, and the recognition is violent, overwhelming. The text does not describe David consoling himself or rationalizing the act. Instead, he is 'smitten'—struck down by his own moral faculty. In the verses that follow (not included in this week's reading but crucial to context), David will explicitly acknowledge that he 'ought not to have done this thing'—suggesting that his conscience is expressing something his reasoning had not yet articulated.

word_study.term_original: וַיַּ֤ךְ לֵב־דָּוִד֙ אֹת֔וֹ (vayyakh lev David oto)
word_study.meaning: The heart (lev) struck/smote (nakhah) him (David). The construction uses 'heart' as the subject and 'him' (David himself) as the object—his own heart is striking him as if his heart were an enemy warrior and David the target. The verb nakhah is the same verb used for striking in battle, for killing with a sword.
word_study.significance: This is the most violent image possible for conscience. The heart, in Hebrew thought, is not merely the seat of emotion but the center of will, judgment, and moral reasoning. David's own moral faculty is treating him as an adversary, striking him down. The use of a martial verb suggests that morality is warfare—not merely a gentle prompter but a force that can strike with violence. A person trained in covenant will have a 'heart' that acts as a warrior on their behalf, fighting against their own transgressions.

word_study.term_original: עַ֚ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּרַ֔ת אֶת־כְּנָ֖ף (al asher karat et kenaf)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'upon/over that which he had cut the corner.' The preposition 'al' (upon, over, concerning) introduces the reason for David's heart striking him. Karat means to cut, to cut off, to sever. Kenaf, as discussed previously, means corner, edge, or wing.
word_study.significance: The narrator does not explain why cutting a corner of cloth should provoke such violent conscience response. The reader is expected to understand implicitly that touching the anointed's garment is a transgression. What is remarkable is not David's act—cutting cloth—but his conscience's interpretation of that act as morally grave. He reads his own action in covenantal terms.

cross_references.connection: Samuel tore Saul's robe to symbolize God's tearing the kingdom from Saul. David's cutting of Saul's corner echoes this act, and David's recoil suggests he recognizes he has acted out a prerogative that belongs only to God and God's ordained prophet.

The verses immediately following (not in this week's reading) have David say to Saul: 'The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my lord, the Lord's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him.' David's conscience is forcing him to articulate why he will not kill—Saul is the Lord's anointed.
'The spirit of man is the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts of the belly.' David's conscience is the light of the Lord within him, searching and revealing his transgression.
Paul writes of his 'conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost.' David's struck heart is this same principle: his conscience, informed by the Spirit, delivers moral judgment.
Alma describes his conscience as smiting him for his sins, using the same metaphor of internal striking. Both David and Alma experience conscience as a force that strikes them with moral violence.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern contexts, the king's garments were understood as extensions of his person and authority. Damage to royal garments had legal and ceremonial significance. In Egyptian, Hittite, and Mesopotamian texts, insult to the king's person included insult to his vestments. The wearing of kingly garments was itself an act of authority—to be allowed to wear or touch the king's garments was a privilege granted only to the closest servants. Samuel's tearing of Saul's robe in 1 Samuel 15 was understood as a prophetic sign-act, and David would have known this precedent. Thus, when David cuts the robe, he may have instinctively recognized that he was either (1) claiming prophetic authority that is not his, or (2) acting out a judgment on Saul that only God could authorize.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:12-14, Alma describes the 'exquisite and bitter pain' of guilt, which comes to a point of 'exceedingly great anxiety.' Alma's anguish mirrors David's heart being struck: both men experience conscience as a force more powerful than external persecution. Alma also shows how this conscience-pain becomes the means of redemption and transformation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:15 promises that the Spirit will 'manifest all things which are expedient unto thee.' David's conscience is this Spirit manifestation—it reveals to him what is and is not expedient in his situation. The principle is that the Holy Ghost becomes an inward witness to what is right.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes language about consecrating oneself to God. David's horror at touching Saul's garment reflects the principle that the anointed—whether king or temple initiate—is consecrated to the Lord and therefore not to be handled by the unanointed. David's struck conscience is his recognition that he has violated a covenant boundary.

commentary.christological_typology: David's internal striking—his conscience dealing him a blow—prefigures the principle of Christ's atonement as self-imposed suffering for transgression. Yet where David suffers for a small act, Christ suffers for all humanity's transgressions. David's struck heart becomes a type of the suffering servant, though David's suffering is infinitesimal compared to Christ's.
commentary.application: Verse 6 contains perhaps the most important lesson in this entire chapter: the trained conscience is a gift more valuable than opportunity or power. David's men see only circumstance and logic; David sees covenant obligation and principle. His conscience does not nag or whisper—it strikes him with force. This suggests several things for modern disciples: First, we should cultivate conscience with the same intentionality that athletes cultivate muscles. Conscience is not static; it is trained through covenant, through scripture study, through prayer, through paying attention to the Holy Ghost's promptings. Second, we should trust our conscience even when it troubles us about actions that cause no apparent external harm. David cutting a piece of cloth harmed no one, yet his conscience was inflamed. This teaches us that moral truth is not utilitarian—whether an action causes harm is not the only measure of its rightness. Third, we should recognize that the Holy Ghost often communicates through sudden, forceful internal clarity rather than through gentle persuasion. When David's heart 'struck' him, the message was unmistakable: stop, you have transgressed. We should pray for such clarity and be willing to accept it even when it comes as an internal blow rather than a comfortable whisper.

text_kjv: And he said unto his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, unto the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed.

commentary.narrative:
David has just cut off the corner of Saul's robe while Saul slept in the cave (verse 4), and his men immediately urge him to kill the king who has been hunting him without cause. This verse captures David's response—a sharp, theologically grounded refusal that establishes the moral architecture of the entire chapter. David does not argue that Saul is innocent, that mercy is pragmatic, or that revenge will backfire. Instead, he invokes God himself as the guarantor of his restraint: 'The LORD forbid'—chalilah li me-YHWH—is an oath formula that binds David before the Almighty. He is not merely expressing reluctance; he is placing his self-control under divine witness.

The repetition of 'the LORD's anointed' twice in a single verse is the theological keystone. David names Saul with ascending theological weight: adoni ('my lord'—a political term of respect), meshiach YHWH ('the LORD's anointed'—the theological title), and then the emphatic repetition meshiach YHWH hu ('the LORD's anointed, he is'). This is not sloppy writing; it is deliberate theological emphasis. David is establishing a principle that will govern his actions through the rest of 1 Samuel and even into 2 Samuel 1, where he executes the man who claims to have killed Saul. The principle is categorical: the anointing places a person in a category that human violence must not presume to touch, regardless of that person's current behavior or fitness to rule.

Crucially, David maintains this posture while hiding from Saul's death squads. This is not sycophancy but covenant respect for the office—David rigorously distinguishes between Saul's personal wickedness (which is real; Saul has tried to murder him repeatedly) and Saul's divinely granted role (which is inviolable). The phrase 'to stretch forth mine hand against him' (lishloch yadi) uses the standard Hebrew idiom for lethal violence. David's men are not proposing to wound or wound or humiliate; they are proposing to kill. And David's refusal is absolute.

word_study.meaning: Far be it from me, God forbid—an oath formula invoking God as guarantor of the speaker's resolve. The root is unclear but the word functions as an intensified negation that places the speaker under divine judgment.
word_study.significance: David does not say 'I will not' but invokes the Lord as the witness to his restraint. This transforms a personal decision into a covenant commitment. The same formula appears when Reuben refuses to murder Joseph (Genesis 37:22) and when Boaz assures Ruth of protection (Ruth 3:11).

word_study.meaning: The LORD's anointed—a construct phrase denoting one whom God has consecrated by the pouring of oil for a specific role. Here, it refers to kingship. The term establishes an inviolable theological category. This is not yet the eschatological Messiah of later Christianity, but it plants the seed: there exists a category of person whom God has set apart, and human hands must not presume to remove what God has installed.
word_study.significance: David uses this term as the foundation of his entire argument in this chapter. It appears twice in verse 7 alone, and recurs in verses 11 and 12. The repetition functions like a legal refrain—David is building a case on a single foundational principle. In the context of Latter-day Saint theology, this establishes the principle of sustaining the Lord's anointed, which reaches its fullest expression in the modern doctrine of sustaining the president of The Church as prophet, seer, and revelator.

word_study.meaning: To extend the hand; the standard Hebrew idiom for violent action, often lethal. The hand extended in violence becomes the hand that does violence.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears multiple times in the narrative of David's life and always signals the potential for lethal harm. By refusing to 'stretch forth his hand,' David refuses the most primal expression of human aggression. The imagery is visceral: the restraint required is physical, not merely mental.

word_study.meaning: My lord, master—a term of political deference and respect for a superior. Used consistently by David for Saul throughout this passage, even during the period when Saul is hunting him.
word_study.significance: David's use of adoni for Saul, even in the moment of having the king at his mercy, demonstrates that his respect is not contingent on Saul's behavior or worthiness. This echoes throughout the chapter and establishes David's character: he honors the office even when the officeholder is unworthy. In Latter-day Saint context, this mirrors the teaching to sustain Church leaders by virtue of their office, not solely on personal merit.

cross_references.connection: David later refuses to kill Saul again, using the identical principle: 'Who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?' This chapter's refusal is not a one-time act but the beginning of a pattern.

After Saul's death, David executes the Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul, saying 'How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?' This shows the principle endured beyond Saul's lifetime.

The Lord commands the Church to sustain the president as 'prophet, seer, and revelator,' establishing the modern covenant equivalent of David's respect for the anointed king. The principle of not laying hands on the Lord's anointed carries forward.
Paul teaches that authorities are 'ordained of God' and resistance to them is resistance to God's ordinance. David's theology of anointing anticipates this New Testament principle.
The Psalm warns, 'Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.' This is the principle David enacts: the anointed are off-limits to human violence.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, kingship was understood as a divinely appointed role. The act of anointing with oil was not merely ceremonial but a binding of the person to God's service. Saul's anointing by Samuel in 1 Samuel 10 created a sacred bond that—in the theology of Israel—could not be severed by human judgment. Even a wicked or unfaithful king retained the protection of this anointing until God himself removed it (as He did through the prophet Samuel in 1 Samuel 15). David's refusal to kill Saul would have been understood by ancient Israelite readers not as weakness but as the highest expression of covenant loyalty and piety. To kill the anointed king would be to usurp God's prerogative; only God could remove what God had installed. This stands in stark contrast to the political norms of surrounding cultures, where assassination of rulers was common and often justified as necessary for the state.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Alma and his followers similarly refuse to raise their hands against the unworthy judges and rulers, respecting the office even when those in office are corrupt. Alma 51:13 describes the refusal to take up arms against those in authority 'over the land.' The principle of sustaining authority—even imperfect authority—runs through Latter-day Saint teaching and is rooted in this Davidic example.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 establishes that the Church sustains the president of the Church as 'prophet, seer, and revelator,' following the pattern David exemplifies here. D&C 76:100-101 describes those who will 'exalt the earth' in the terrestrial kingdom—among them those who 'received not the testimony of Jesus...but afterwards received it.' The principle of sustaining God's anointed, even when one must wait for God's timing and correction, is central to LDS covenant life. D&C 58:21-22 teaches that those who act without being commanded receive no reward, which supports David's principle: removing the anointed is God's prerogative, not man's.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The anointing of kings in the Old Testament prefigures the anointing of the Savior and the anointing ordinances in the temple. In the temple, members make covenants to sustain constituted authority and to use their agency in harmony with God's will, not in opposition to it. The principle that certain persons and ordinances are sacred and not to be violated by human hands is foundational to temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: David's refusal to lay hands on the anointed king, despite the king's unfitness and aggression, prefigures Christ's refusal to call down judgment on His enemies. When Christ was arrested, Peter drew his sword to protect Him (John 18:10), but Jesus rebuked him: 'Put up again thy sword into his place' (Matthew 26:52). Just as David recognized that vengeance belongs to God, Christ recognized that judgment belongs to the Father. Both David and Christ exemplify the principle that covenant loyalty sometimes means bearing injustice rather than taking personal vengeance. Moreover, David's respect for Saul's anointing, despite Saul's unworthiness, points to the theology of Christ as the ultimately anointed one—the Messiah whose anointing cannot be undone by human opposition or rejection.
commentary.application: In Latter-day Saint life, this verse establishes a principle that extends beyond literal kingship to all sustaining of authority—ecclesiastical, familial, civic. When you sustain the president of The Church, you are not primarily making a judgment about his personal worthiness or popularity; you are honoring the office and the anointing to which he is called, similar to how David honored the anointing on Saul despite Saul's murderous behavior. This does not mean unquestioning obedience or enablement of genuine evil, but it does mean a refusal to undermine or seek to overthrow constituted authority through private judgment or violence. Where modern Latter-day Saints struggle most is in holding together two truths simultaneously: (1) the authority is sacred and divinely appointed, and (2) the person in authority is fallible and may require correction. David models this balance perfectly. He does not pretend Saul is innocent; he simply refuses to be the instrument of Saul's removal. That belongs to God. How do you sustain imperfect authority in your own sphere? Do you distinguish between respecting the office and enabling the person's faults?

text_kjv: So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul. But Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative shifts from David's theological pronouncement to the practical consequences. David's words are not gentle persuasion but forceful action: he 'tore into his men' (vayshassa—the root means to split or rend, used elsewhere for tearing apart animals) with this theological argument. His men are not convinced by abstract principle; they are subdued by the intensity and authority of David's rebuke. David's verbal restraint of his men required as much force and determination as killing Saul would have required, only channeled in the opposite direction. He does not merely request that they refrain; he commands them not to rise against Saul, using authority to enforce his will against theirs.

Meanwhile, Saul rises and departs in complete ignorance of his narrow escape. The narrator's spare statement—'Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way'—emphasizes the dramatic irony that will dominate verses 9-12. Saul walks out alive without knowing that his life was held in another man's hands and returned to him by an act of covenant loyalty he cannot even perceive. This is one of the great dramatic ironies in biblical narrative: the man who has hunted David relentlessly, convinced that David seeks his death, leaves the very moment when David had the power to kill him but chose not to. Saul's departure is narrated with flat, almost dismissive language—he simply goes his way, completely unaware of the grace he has received.

word_study.meaning: He tore, he split, he rebuked sharply. The root shasa means to rend or split apart, used of violent tearing. The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'tore into,' preserving the verbal force.
word_study.significance: The KJV's 'stayed' is far too mild and masks the intensity of David's action. David did not gently persuade; he violently rebuked his men's intention. The use of a root meaning 'to tear' suggests that David's words had the force of a physical intervention—he split apart their argument, their will, their plan. This is the only occurrence of this verb in 1 Samuel, making it a unique choice for describing the intensity of David's restraint.

word_study.meaning: And he did not give/allow them. The verb natan (to give, to allow, to permit) here means to permit or authorize. David actively prevented his men from acting.
word_study.significance: This is not passive restraint or moral suasion that the men could accept or reject. David uses his authority as leader to actively prevent them from rising against Saul. He commands their obedience. This establishes David's hierarchy of loyalty: his loyalty to God (expressed through respect for the anointing) overrides his men's demands and his own potential inclinations.

word_study.meaning: He rose, he got up. Used for both Saul's physical rising from sleep and the potential for the men to 'rise against' (rise up to attack) Saul.
word_study.significance: The same verb is used for Saul's actual rising and the men's potential rising—a linguistic parallel that underscores the dramatic irony. Saul rises in literal fact; the men rise only in thwarted intention. The verb 'rise against' is a common idiom for rebellion or violent action.

cross_references.connection: Immediately before this verse, David's heart smote him for cutting off the corner of Saul's robe—showing his own internal conflict between what his men urge and what his conscience allows. Verse 8 shows how he resolves that conflict: by forcefully commanding his men to obey his conscience.

The same root (shasa, to tear) is used when Samson tears a lion apart: 'he rent him as he would have rent a kid.' David's tearing into his men's argument with words has the same force as Samson's physical rending.

'He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down and without walls.' David's strict command of his men demonstrates the self-rule and internal governance required of a true leader.

The Lord teaches that 'he that seeketh to save his life shall lose it; and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.' David's forceful redirection of his men away from killing Saul demonstrates that restraint in favor of God's anointed is itself a form of covenant obedience.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, loyalty to a leader often meant personal devotion to the leader's interests, which frequently included the elimination of rivals or threats. David's men are responding from within that cultural logic: Saul is David's enemy and has hunted him; therefore, Saul should be eliminated. David's refusal to permit this would have struck them as inexplicable without understanding the Israelite theology of anointing. The fact that David's men even make the suggestion shows how far removed they were from David's covenant perspective. By forcefully rebuking them, David is not merely making a personal choice; he is teaching his own court a fundamental principle about the sanctity of God's anointed. This will become crucial for understanding his reign when he becomes king—his court will consist of men who have been trained in this principle.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma demonstrates similar leadership when he restrains his followers from violence. In Alma 1, when dissidents arise and persecute believers, Alma does not permit his people to take up arms in defense but instead takes the matter to the judges and later to the Church leadership. The principle of sustaining constituted authority even under provocation appears throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:23-48 discusses the principle of forgiving those who repent and of patient suffering under injustice, which is the principle David enacts here. The revelation teaches that believers should appeal to the law and to authority rather than taking personal vengeance. David's forceful restraint of his men aligns with this later revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes a promise to sustain those placed in authority and to submit to the priesthood order. David's enforcement of this principle among his men foreshadows the way the Church teaches that covenant members sustain the priesthood authority of the Church.

commentary.christological_typology: David's restraint of his men from killing Saul prefigures Christ's restraint of His disciples. In Matthew 26:51-52, when Peter strikes the servant of the high priest during Jesus's arrest, Jesus rebukes him: 'Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.' Like David commanding his men not to rise against the anointed king, Jesus commands His followers not to defend the anointed one through violence. Both recognize that God's purposes work through submission and suffering, not through taking matters into human hands.
commentary.application: This verse challenges Latter-day Saints to examine how they restrain their own impulses and those of others toward taking unauthorized action. If you are a parent, do you command obedience to righteous principles even when your children want to act according to their own judgment? If you are a leader in the Church, do you use your authority to uphold the principle of sustaining constituted authority, even when circumstances tempt others to criticism or rebellion? If you are a member of the Church, do you allow yourself to be 'stayed' by the words of leaders who invoke principle higher than your immediate interests? David's intense, forceful restraint suggests that covenant loyalty sometimes requires standing against the opinions of those closest to us. Who are the people in your life urging you to act in ways that would violate your deeper covenant commitments?

text_kjv: David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave, and cried after Saul, saying, My lord the king. And when Saul looked behind him, David stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself.

commentary.narrative: After David has restrained his men and Saul has left the cave, David emerges to pursue him—not to attack, but to reveal the truth. The verse describes a carefully choreographed scene that unfolds visually in the desert landscape. David calls out 'My lord the king!' (Adoni hammelekh), establishing the tone immediately: this is not the voice of a rival claiming the throne, but of a vassal acknowledging his sovereign. Saul turns to look, and in that moment of turning, David performs a public act of profound humility. He knells—or stoops—with his face to the ground and bows, simultaneously exposing himself to any attack Saul might attempt while demonstrating absolute subjection. This physical posture mirrors the theological posture David established in verse 7: the anointed king is beyond reproach, and David will not raise himself against him even in appearance. The passage is narrated with cinematic precision: each action is visible and unambiguous in the desert light.

word_study.meaning: He called after, he cried out after. The verb kara (to call, to cry) with the preposition achrei (after) indicates calling to someone departing.
word_study.significance: The verb 'to cry' suggests urgency and intensity—David is not speaking quietly but calling aloud across the desert to get Saul's attention. This is a public declaration, not a private word. The phrase 'cried after' appears elsewhere when someone pursues another with urgent words, often in contexts of warning or critical information.

word_study.meaning: My lord, the king. A double title combining the personal term of respect (adoni, my lord) with the official title (hammelekh, the king). This is David's standard form of address for Saul throughout these verses.
word_study.significance: David addresses Saul consistently as 'my lord the king,' never as 'Saul,' never as a rival, never as the man hunting him. The title affirms Saul's legitimacy and David's subordination. This is not performance but David's genuine theological stance: regardless of Saul's actions, the office is sacred.

word_study.meaning: He bowed, he knelt, he stooped. The verb kana (to bend, to bow, to stoop) describes the physical posture of submission and respect. The same verb is used for bowing before God.
word_study.significance: David's posture is one of absolute submission—face to earth, completely exposed and vulnerable. This is the posture of a vassal before a king, a worshipper before God. By making himself utterly vulnerable, David demonstrates the genuineness of his submission. Any appearance of threat is removed. He has disabled himself to remove any pretext for Saul to strike.

word_study.meaning: He prostrated himself, he bowed down. The verb shachah (to bow, to prostrate) is used for worship and for the deepest form of submission. In Genesis 37:7-10, Joseph's brothers bow to him; in 1 Samuel 28:14, Saul bows to the spirit of Samuel.
word_study.significance: This is not a casual nod but full prostration—the posture of worship or absolute subjection. By prostrating himself, David makes clear that his submission to Saul's kingship is as complete as his submission to God. The anointing makes this appropriate: to honor the anointed is to honor God's choice.

cross_references.connection: Joseph's brothers bow before him in his dream: 'We were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves made obeisance to my sheaf.' David's bowing to Saul is genuine obeisance, unlike Joseph's dream which prophesied future reversal of order.

Abigail uses the same posture—stooping with her face to the earth, bowing low—when she approaches David to intercede for her household. The same verb (kana) and posture signal urgent appeal and submission.

David writes, 'I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD.' His public bowing before Saul demonstrates the same commitment to maintain innocence and right relationship with God that characterizes his prayers.

Members are commanded to 'give heed unto all his [the president's] words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me; for his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth.' David's posture of absolute submission to the anointed king prefigures this covenant.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern court culture, the physical posture of a vassal toward a king communicated political truth. Bowing, kneeling, and prostration were not mere courtesy but legal expressions of subordination and loyalty. By prostrating himself, David is making a public, legally binding statement: 'I acknowledge your kingship. I am not your rival. I do not claim what is yours.' For a man who has been hunted and who will eventually become king himself, this act of physical submission is an extraordinary gesture. It would have been witnessed by Saul's attendants and would have become knowledge that spread through both courts. David is using his body as a text to communicate his theological principles.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 27, after Alma the Younger's conversion, he makes restitution for the damage he has caused, humbling himself before those he has persecuted. Similarly, in Alma 36, Alma describes his conversion in language of complete submission—'I did humble myself.' David's physical humiliation before Saul, despite having power over him, demonstrates the internal humility that precedes true conversion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 4:4 teaches 'Remember faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, brotherly kindness, godliness, charity, humility, diligence.' David's act of bowing demonstrates humility—maintaining it despite power. D&C 38:28 teaches 'I say unto you, be one; and prepare yourselves, and be ye ready.' David's public submission through his posture prepares him for the kingship he will eventually receive by making clear that leadership is not about personal elevation but about serving God's anointed purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, members assume postures of humility and submission before God—kneeling in prayer, standing with arms raised in certain positions. David's voluntary assumption of a posture of utter submission to Saul (the Lord's anointed) mirrors the stance of covenant submission that the temple teaches.

commentary.christological_typology: David's voluntary assumption of a posture of humiliation before Saul, while in a position of power, prefigures Christ's voluntary humiliation. Philippians 2:7-8 describes how Christ 'made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant...and humbled himself, and became obedient unto death.' Like Christ, David uses his position of power to assume a position of submission rather than dominance. Both demonstrate that true strength expresses itself through voluntary submission to God's purposes, not through grasping for authority.
commentary.application: What does your posture—literal and metaphorical—communicate about your submission to constituted authority? When you sustain a leader in the Church, do you do so merely with words, or does your stance, your tone, your body language reinforce your words? David teaches that genuine respect for the Lord's anointed is embodied—it shows up in how you present yourself, not just in what you say. Consider how you speak about and to your leaders, your parents, those in authority over you. Does your demeanor reinforce that you recognize their office as sacred, or does it convey that you are withholding true submission, waiting to see if they prove worthy? David's bowing to Saul without knowing whether Saul would strike him down demonstrates a vulnerability that is the mark of genuine respect. Can you practice that kind of vulnerability in your submission?

text_kjv: And David said to Saul, Wherefore hearest thou men's words, saying, Behold, David seeketh thy hurt?

commentary.narrative:
Having demonstrated his physical submission through prostration, David now begins his defense with a rhetorical strategy designed to separate Saul from the slanderers who poison his thinking. David does not address the substance of the accusation directly—whether he is actually seeking Saul's harm. Instead, he questions the source of Saul's conviction: 'Why do you listen to the words of people who say...' The phrase 'men's words' (divrei adam) places emphasis on hearsay, rumor, the testimony of others, as opposed to what Saul can verify with his own eyes. David's defense will rest on shifting Saul from reliance on what others tell him to reliance on visible evidence.

This is psychologically astute: Saul has been listening to people who claim David seeks his death. These people may include courtiers who benefit from Saul's paranoia, or generals who fear David's military success, or others with ulterior motives. David's opening move is to ask Saul to question his sources. The accusation itself—that David is 'seeking to harm you'—echoes the language of verse 5 where David's men say 'God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand,' and verse 11 where David points out that Saul is the one 'hunting' David. David will turn the accusation around: it is not David who is seeking, but Saul. Yet before making that reversal explicit, David first asks Saul to consider: what is the basis of your conviction? Are you relying on truth you have seen with your own eyes, or on words you have heard from others?

The verb 'seeketh' (mevaqesh) is significant because it is the same verb used in verse 3 for Saul's search for David: 'Saul sought him every day.' The irony is sharp: Saul is actively searching for David while accusing David of seeking his harm. But David leaves this irony implicit here, allowing Saul to discover it through the evidence David is about to present.

word_study.meaning: You hear, you listen to, you heed. The verb shama (to hear, to listen, to obey) can mean passive hearing or active heeding—taking to heart what one hears.
word_study.significance: David is not merely asking whether Saul hears words; he is asking why Saul heeds them, takes them seriously, allows them to shape his actions. The question implies a critique: why would you give credence to mere words when you could verify truth with your own eyes?

word_study.meaning: The words of men, human speech, hearsay. The phrase emphasizes the merely human, unreliable nature of rumor and report as opposed to direct evidence.
word_study.significance: By calling them 'men's words,' David immediately signals that these are not divine utterances, not prophetic words, not verified fact, but merely what people say. This opens space for Saul to reconsider whether he should trust them more than his own observation.

word_study.meaning: Is seeking your harm/evil. The verb baqash (to seek, to search for) paired with ra'ah (evil, harm, misfortune) creates a phrase meaning to pursue someone's destruction or injury.
word_study.significance: This is the accusation David is addressing: that he actively pursues Saul's harm. David will spend the rest of his speech demonstrating that the opposite is true—he has the opportunity to harm Saul and has deliberately chosen not to.

cross_references.connection: The verse establishes that 'Saul sought him every day,' using the same verb (baqash) for seeking that verse 10 uses for the accusation that David seeks Saul. David is reversing the direction of the seeking.
'The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.' David appeals to Saul to be prudent and wise by seeking to verify what he hears rather than accepting hearsay.
'The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.' David challenges Saul to be prudent rather than simple—to look to the evidence rather than believe every word.

'And let all thy people in every congregation gather together their monies and send it up unto the land of Zion...that they are not idle.' The principle of personal verification and direct observation rather than reliance on hearsay appears in Latter-day revelation as well—members are encouraged to seek direct knowledge.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern court, information flowed through a hierarchy of courtiers, servants, and officials. A king's understanding of reality was heavily mediated by what his advisors told him. Saul's court appears to have been rife with factionalism—courtiers with competing interests all vying for the king's ear. David's rhetorical strategy of asking Saul to distinguish between hearsay and evidence is an appeal to the king's better judgment. An ancient audience would have recognized the problem David is addressing: courts are notoriously vulnerable to manipulation through rumor and false accusation. A wise king verifies with his own eyes and with trustworthy witnesses. David is implicitly appealing to Saul's identity as one who should be beyond such manipulation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 5:51-52, Alma asks the people, 'Have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances?' He is calling them to verify their spiritual state through personal experience rather than hearsay or social conformity. Similarly, David calls Saul to verify the truth about David's intentions through direct evidence rather than report.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 91:1-2 teaches that 'the Church, being driven to desperation, shall call upon the Lord, and his voice shall be heard from heaven.' The principle of direct relationship with God rather than reliance solely on intermediaries runs through Latter-day revelation. D&C 9:7-8 teaches that God communicates through feeling and understanding, inviting personal verification. David invites Saul to verify through observation rather than trusting only what others report.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, members encounter the covenants and ordinances directly rather than merely hearing about them from others. The temple invitation is to personal, direct participation and witnessing rather than reliance on secondhand report of what happens within the temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus frequently faced the same problem: people judging Him based on what others said rather than on direct observation of His works. In John 7:24, Jesus says, 'Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.' Like David, Jesus calls His listeners to look beyond hearsay and prejudice to the evidence before them. In Matthew 11:4-5, when John the Baptist sends disciples to ask if Jesus is the Messiah, Jesus responds by pointing to the works they can see: 'The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.' Like David, Christ appeals to visible evidence over rumor.
commentary.application: In an age of information overload, David's challenge to Saul is profoundly relevant: on what basis do you believe what you believe about others? Are you relying on direct observation and verified evidence, or on what you have heard from sources with their own agendas? In your family, your church, your community, do you participate in spreading 'men's words'—rumors, accusations, secondhand reports—without verifying them? Do you judge your leaders, your fellow church members, your family members based on what others say about them, or do you seek to verify through your own observation and direct communication? David models a principle: when you are accused of seeking to harm someone, the appropriate response is not to defend through words alone but to provide evidence. How can you live this principle? If someone has spoken against you, can you let your actions provide the evidence of your true character? If you have heard rumors about someone else, are you willing to seek direct evidence before accepting the accusation?

text_kjv: Behold, this day thine eyes have seen how that the LORD had delivered thee to day into mine hand in the cave: and some bade me kill thee: but mine eye spared thee; and I said, I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD's anointed.

commentary.narrative:
David now provides the visible evidence he promised. The phrase 'your eyes have seen' (ra'u einekha) appeals to Saul's personal observation of facts that cannot be disputed. David is in the cave with the king—a fact that requires explanation. If David had ambitions to kill Saul, the circumstance was perfect: Saul alone (or nearly alone), defenseless in sleep, in a cave where witnesses are few. David acknowledges that someone urged him to kill Saul—likely referring to the collective pressure from his men in verse 5, though the Hebrew allows ambiguity about whether it was the men or David's own conscience speaking. David then reports his own internal dialogue: he says 'I spared' (vattachas aleikha—literally 'my eye/he had compassion on you') and quotes himself: 'I will not stretch out my hand against my lord; for he is the LORD's anointed.'

This third invocation of 'the LORD's anointed' (meshiach YHWH) is the climax of David's argument. He has now stated the principle three times: verse 7 (twice), verse 11. The repetition functions like a legal citation—David is grounding his defense not in prudence or mercy, but in a single foundational theological principle: the anointing is inviolable. The principle is not situational; it does not depend on Saul's worthiness or current behavior. It is categorical and universal. Whoever bears the LORD's anointing is protected from human violence by the will of God Himself.

The phrase 'this very day' (hayom hazo) emphasizes that this is not ancient history but a present demonstration. Saul can verify it now, in this moment, by the fact that David is standing before him alive and free, having had every opportunity and reason to kill him but having chosen covenant loyalty instead.

word_study.meaning: Your eyes have seen—an appeal to personal, visual verification. The verb ra'ah (to see) emphasizes direct observation rather than hearsay.
word_study.significance: David is moving Saul from reliance on what others tell him (verse 10) to reliance on what he has personally witnessed. This is the epistemological shift David has been attempting throughout: from hearsay to evidence, from others' words to direct observation.

word_study.meaning: Gave you to me, placed you into my hand. The verb natan (to give) attributes the situation to God's action.
word_study.significance: David does not claim credit for maneuvering Saul into the cave. He attributes the circumstance to God. The implication is: God placed Saul in my hands—this was divine arrangement, not human strategy. And God placed him there to test whether I would honor His anointing. David passed the test.

word_study.meaning: Had compassion on you, looked with pity and spared. The verb chasah means to look with pity, to have compassion, to show mercy by refraining from harm.
word_study.significance: The subject of the verb is ambiguous—it could be 'my eye' (implying David's merciful gaze) or David himself (implied from context). The unusual phrasing creates a poetic effect: David's eye—the faculty that could have guided his hand to kill—instead guided his hand away from killing. Mercy resided in his seeing, not in deliberate calculation.

word_study.meaning: The LORD's anointed—the person consecrated by God through anointing for a divinely appointed role. This is the third occurrence in the chapter (after two in verse 7).
word_study.significance: The repetition of this phrase across three verses (appearing four times total) is the organizing principle of David's entire defense. Each time he invokes it, he is asserting the same principle: the anointing creates an inviolable category. This is the foundation, not mercy, not prudence, not even the injustice of Saul's hunting him. The foundation is: God has anointed Saul, therefore human violence must not touch him.

cross_references.connection: Samuel anointed Saul as king on God's command. The anointing that David now honors was performed by the prophet Samuel in God's name, establishing Saul's divine appointment.

'Recompense to no man evil for evil...Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.' David's refusal to avenge himself on Saul enacts the principle Paul later articulates: vengeance belongs to God, not to private judgment.

'Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide.' David's invocation of his own integrity and restraint parallels his later psalmody about maintaining innocence before God.

'Therefore, renounce war and proclaim peace, and seek diligently to turn the hearts of the children of men, the armies of the wicked, from the violence and bloodshed. Therefore, renounce war and proclaim peace.' David's choice not to 'stretch forth his hand' against Saul embodies the principle later revealed in the Doctrine and Covenants.
Alma and his followers refuse to 'take up arms' against 'constituted authority,' maintaining loyalty to office even when those in office are unworthy. This is the same principle David enacts.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the concept of divine kingship meant that the king was not merely a political functionary but a sacred person—set apart by divine action (in Israel's case, through anointing with oil by a prophet). To strike the king was not merely a political act but a sacrilege, a violation of the sacred order. David's appeal to the anointing would have resonated powerfully with ancient Near Eastern audiences, for whom the sanctity of the anointed king was a fundamental principle. However, Israel's theology was distinctive in maintaining this principle even when the king was unjust or incompetent. Other cultures might have justified the removal of a bad king; Israel's theology insisted that even a bad king retained the protection of his anointing until God Himself removed it (which happened in Saul's case through David's kingship, but not through David's hand).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 4:19-20, Alma steps down from the judgment seat to preach full-time. Though he has authority, he uses it not to grasp for power but to serve. Later, in Alma 51:13, the people choose not to take up arms against 'those who had been appointed to conduct the affairs of the state...notwithstanding their unrighteousness,' maintaining respect for office despite disapproval of the officeholder. This is the same principle David enacts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that Church members are to sustain the president as 'prophet, seer, and revelator,' binding themselves 'by the authority of the Holy Ghost, which he hath received.' The principle of sustaining the Lord's anointed—respecting the office by virtue of the sacred appointment—is foundational to Latter-day Saint covenant life. D&C 58:21-22 teaches that those who act 'in all things by the consent of their children, and also my servants your stewards' will receive the approbation of God. David's refusal to act without God's consent (by stretching forth his hand when God forbade it) exemplifies this principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes a promise to sustain the priesthood authority of the Church. Just as David sustains Saul by virtue of his anointing despite Saul's unworthiness, temple members covenant to sustain the priesthood authority of the Church, trusting that God, not human judgment, has established this order.

commentary.christological_typology: David's three-fold invocation of 'the LORD's anointed' as the reason for his restraint prefigures the New Testament understanding of Christ as the ultimate Anointed One—the Messiah who bears the full weight of God's consecration. As David would not raise his hand against Saul despite provocation, the disciples of Christ do not raise their hands against Him despite injustice (Matthew 26:51-52). The principle is the same: the anointed belongs to God, and human violence against the anointed is transgression against God Himself. Moreover, David's refusal to claim kingship by force, even when opportunity arose, prefigures Christ's refusal to claim His kingdom through the political means others offered (John 18:36). Both David and Christ demonstrate that true kingship is conferred by God, not seized by force.
commentary.application: This verse cuts to the heart of Latter-day Saint covenant life: Do you sustain the Lord's anointed? Not because you find them perfect, not because they make decisions you agree with, not because they demonstrate personal worthiness that persuades you—but because they are the Lord's anointed. David's principle applies: the anointing is inviolable. If you find yourself tempted to undermine, criticize, or work against the president of The Church or other priesthood leaders, you are effectively trying to 'stretch forth your hand' against the Lord's anointed. David's test was acute—he had literal power of life and death over Saul. Your test is more subtle: you have the power of voice and influence. Will you use that power against the Lord's anointed, or will you 'spare' them through your restraint, your covenant loyalty, your refusal to participate in speaking against them? What would it mean for you to invoke David's principle in your own life: 'I will not stretch out my hand against the Lord's anointed'?
