text_kjv: Moreover, my father, see, yea, see the skirt of thy robe in my hand: for in that I cut off the skirt of thy robe, and killed thee not, know thou and see that there is neither evil nor transgression in mine hand, and I have not sinned against thee; yet thou huntest my soul to take it.

commentary.narrative:
David moves from abstract principle to concrete evidence. He addresses Saul as 'my father' (avi), shifting from the formal 'my lord the king' to an intimate, familial address that invokes the father-in-law relationship and appeals to Saul's paternal instinct. The doubled imperative 'see, yes see!' (re'eh gam re'eh) demands visual verification. David then displays the physical evidence: the 'corner of your robe' (kenaf me'ilekha) in his own hand. This is the same corner he cut off in verse 4, the symbol of David's restraint. The piece of robe serves a double function: practically, it proves David was close enough to kill; symbolically, it shows David holding a piece of Saul's royal authority and voluntarily returning it unharmed.

David then offers three comprehensive denials: 'neither evil nor transgression' (ein ra'ah vafesha) 'and I have not sinned against thee' (velo chatati lekha). These three terms cover the full range of wrongdoing—malicious intent (ra'ah, 'evil'), covenant breach (pesha, 'rebellion/transgression'), and moral failure (chet, 'sin'). Against this comprehensive assertion of innocence, David sets Saul's relentless pursuit: 'yet thou huntest my soul to take it' (ve'atah tzodeh et nafshi leqachtah). The verb 'huntest' (tzodeh) casts Saul as a predator stalking prey. David is the hunted animal, not the aggressor. By juxtaposing his own innocence with Saul's predatory pursuit, David forces Saul to confront an inversion: the man who has been hunting you down is the one seeking your death, not the man standing before you with your own robe in his hand.

This verse is David's final appeal, the climax of his defense. He has moved from theological principle (the anointing is inviolable) to internal evidence (I had opportunity to kill you and did not) to external evidence (your own robe proves my restraint) to moral assertion (I am innocent of all wrongdoing) to a reversal of the accusation (you are the hunter, I am the hunted). The accumulation of evidence and argument is designed to break through Saul's paranoia and accusation with the force of truth.

word_study.meaning: My father—a term of intimate relationship and respect. Used here in the father-in-law relationship (David had married Saul's daughter Michal).
word_study.significance: This is the only time in this chapter that David uses 'father' for Saul. The shift from 'my lord the king' to 'my father' is a rhetorical move designed to appeal to Saul's paternal instinct and to invoke the natural bond of family. David is also implicitly highlighting the monstrosity of Saul's behavior: a father hunting his own son's life is a perversion of the natural order.

word_study.meaning: See—yes, see! The doubled imperative with the intensifying particle gam ('also, indeed, yes') creates urgent, repeated demand for visual verification.
word_study.significance: The doubled imperative mimics oral speech, the insistence of someone trying to break through another person's blindness or refusal to see. David is trying to force Saul to witness the truth with his own eyes.

word_study.meaning: Corner/edge/wing of your robe. The kanaf (corner, edge, wing) of the royal garment is the piece David cut off. The word kanaf can also mean 'wing,' creating an image of David holding the 'wing' or extension of Saul's royal garment.
word_study.significance: The 'corner' of the king's robe becomes the symbol of kingship itself—David holds a piece of Saul's royal authority in his hand and returns it. This is symbolic language suggesting that kingship itself is being torn from Saul (fulfilling God's decree in 1 Samuel 15 that the kingdom would be torn from Saul), but not by David's hand. David will not be the instrument of that tearing; God alone will accomplish it.

word_study.meaning: Evil, harm, misfortune. A broad term for wickedness, malice, or malicious intent.
word_study.significance: This is the first term in David's triple denial: no malicious intent has animated his action. David is asserting not just that he did not kill Saul, but that he harbored no malice toward him.

word_study.meaning: Transgression, rebellion, covenant breach. A term denoting willful violation of a binding agreement, not accidental wrongdoing.
word_study.significance: This is the second term in David's triple denial: he has not broken covenant with Saul. Pesha is a stronger term than ordinary sin—it implies deliberate violation of a solemn bond. David is asserting that his covenant loyalty to Saul has remained intact despite Saul's aggression.

word_study.meaning: I have sinned—the verb chet means to miss the mark, to err, to transgress. The most general term for moral failure.
word_study.significance: This is the third term in David's triple denial: no moral failure, no err, no transgression against Saul. The three-term denial (ra'ah, pesha, chet) echoes judicial oath formulas where an accused person categorically clears himself of all charges.

word_study.meaning: Hunt, pursue. The verb tsad means to hunt, to pursue as prey. Saul's pursuit is imaged as predatory hunting.
word_study.significance: By using the verb 'hunt,' David inverts the moral positions: David is the prey, not the aggressor. Saul is the hunter. This reversal is crucial to David's argument—he is not the one seeking Saul's death; Saul is the one seeking David's death.

word_study.meaning: To take, to seize, to capture. The verb laqach with the sense of taking someone's life.
word_study.significance: Saul is pursuing David not to talk, not to recruit him, but to 'take' his life. The phrase 'hunt my soul to take it' (tzodeh et nafshi leqachtah) describes deliberate, sustained effort to accomplish David's death.

cross_references.connection: Samuel tells Saul, 'The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.' David's holding of Saul's robe while not killing him symbolizes the tearing of the kingdom that God has already decreed but not yet accomplished through David.

Saul's pursuit of David began because David's military success made Saul afraid: 'What can he have more but the kingdom?' David's refusal to grasp the kingdom by killing Saul demonstrates his respect for the divinely appointed order, even as Saul's fear drives him to hunt David.

David writes, 'O LORD my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me...Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces.' This psalm likely reflects the period when Saul hunted him, and David appeals to God rather than taking vengeance into his own hands.

The passage lists things the Lord hates, including 'hands that shed innocent blood' and 'he that soweth discord among brethren.' David asserts his innocence ('neither evil nor transgression') in these very terms—he has not shed innocent blood, has not sown discord through false accusation.

'And this ye might have supposed that he would have exercised his power, according to the flesh; but behold, I say unto you, He hath exercised his power in the flesh indeed, but not to your condemnation.' Just as David exercises power (having Saul in his power) but not in condemnation, Christ exercises His power not to condemn but to save.

Alma steps down from power, saying 'Now I say unto you, that the foundation of the destruction of this people is to get gain and to get riches, and to get glory; and that they despise the poor.' David, by refusing to grasp the kingdom through killing Saul, demonstrates the opposite principle: respect for God's order over personal gain.

commentary.historical_context: The royal robe was a sign of kingship and authority in the ancient Near East. The cutting of the robe had symbolic significance—it represented either the tearing of the kingdom (as later happens to Saul through Samuel) or the vulnerability of kingship. By cutting the corner and then returning it, David performs a symbolic action that communicates his respect for Saul's kingship even as he demonstrates the fragility of that kingship. For an ancient audience, a vassal displaying a piece of the king's garment would have carried the weight of a legal demonstration. David is quite literally holding the evidence of his power and his restraint in his hand. The fact that Saul can see this evidence, can touch it, can verify it with his own eyes, gives David's defense an irrefutable quality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 5:21-24, Nephi describes how his people prosper while Laman and Lemuel rebel, yet Nephi maintains covenant loyalty. Later, in Mosiah 24, Alma and his followers are afflicted by King Noah, yet they do not rise up against him but appeal to God. Even when oppressed by constituted authority, the righteous in the Book of Mormon maintain their covenant loyalty, like David with Saul.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26-27 teaches 'He who is idle shall not eat the bread nor wear the garments of the laborer.' David, by working to sustain Saul's kingship (through his covenant loyalty) rather than seizing it, labors for the maintenance of God's order. D&C 121:45-46 teaches that the 'increase of dominion...comes by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned, by kindness, and pure knowledge.' David's approach to power—refusing to grasp it, showing restraint, appealing to conscience—exemplifies these principles.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members promise to sustain priesthood authority and to submit to divine order. David's triple denial of wrongdoing (no evil, no transgression, no sin) parallels the purity required of those entering into sacred covenants. His voluntary submission to Saul's authority, despite having power to overthrow him, mirrors the covenant promise to sustain those placed in authority.

commentary.christological_typology: David's display of the piece of Saul's robe—his voluntary restraint while holding power, his appeal to innocence, his refusal to grasp the kingdom—prefigures Christ's surrender of rights and power. Philippians 2:6-8 describes Christ as one who 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant.' Like David, Christ had the power to claim what was His by right (the kingdom) but chose instead to submit to the Father's will. David's triple assertion of innocence—no evil, no transgression, no sin—points to the sinlessness of Christ, who made 'no sin' (2 Corinthians 5:21) and who appeals to the Father: 'I have not sinned.' Both David and Christ allow their actions (not merely their words) to testify to their innocence and their covenant loyalty.
commentary.application: This verse forces a confrontation with a difficult truth: you may be innocent, you may have done nothing to harm someone who accuses you, you may have exercised restraint when you had power to act otherwise—and still that person may pursue you with accusations and hunting. David offers no guarantee that his demonstration of the robe will change Saul's mind. In fact, the narrative suggests it does not—Saul's paranoia continues. Yet David presents the evidence anyway, trusting that he has done what is right before God. For modern covenant members, this teaches a profound lesson: your integrity, your restraint, your covenant loyalty may not persuade those who are determined to believe accusations against you. You cannot control their response. But you can, like David, ensure that your conduct is genuinely innocent—that you harbor no evil intent, that you have not broken covenant, that you have not sinned against them. You can, like David, voluntarily display your integrity and trust God with the outcome. Are there people in your life who hunt you with accusations despite your innocence? Can you, like David, maintain your own covenant loyalty and righteousness even when it is not appreciated or believed?

text_kjv: And thou hast shewed this day how that thou hast dealt well with me: forasmuch as when the LORD had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not.

commentary.narrative: Saul's words here mark a profound moment of recognition. After David spared his life in the cave, Saul understands what has just happened: he was entirely at David's mercy, completely enclosed in David's power (the Hebrew *sagar* suggests God 'shutting' or 'handing over' Saul to David the way a gate closes around a prisoner), and David chose mercy instead of vengeance. This is not merely an emotional response but a conscious acknowledgment of David's restraint and character. Saul uses the word *higadta*—'you have shown,' a Hiphil form that implies public disclosure—suggesting that David's act was not a private kindness but a visible, undeniable demonstration of moral superiority. Saul sees David's choice not to kill him as evidence of *tov*, goodness that transcends survival instinct and self-interest.
commentary.narrative_cont: What makes this verse theologically significant is Saul's explicit attribution of his deliverance to the LORD. He does not say 'You had me in your power and spared me' but rather 'The LORD had delivered me into your hand, and you did not kill me.' This grammar matters: God is the primary agent who handed Saul over; David is the secondary agent who chose not to act. Saul is beginning to see the hand of God in his own predicament—not as punishment yet (that will come later in his final descent), but as a test of David's worthiness. The irony cuts deep: Saul has spent months trying to kill David, and in a single moment, when David could have reversed their positions and killed Saul, Saul recognizes that David is the righteous man and Saul has been the pursuer of innocent blood.
commentary.narrative_cont2: This confession is sincere in the moment, yet the narrative arc will show that sincerity and lasting change are not the same thing. Saul will soon resume his pursuit of David. The text does not psychoanalyze Saul's contradictions—it simply records his words and leaves the reader to grapple with the mystery of human inconsistency. A man can be genuinely moved, genuinely acknowledge truth, and then return to his former patterns. This is not hypocrisy so much as the tragic reality of a man at war with himself, divided between the spirit and the flesh, between what he knows to be right and what his fear compels him to do.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil form of nagad, meaning 'to make known, to declare, to show.' The Hiphil intensifies the sense: not merely to know something privately, but to make it publicly manifest, to put it on display.
word_study.significance: David's act of mercy was not hidden or subtle—it was a deliberate, visible demonstration. In The Covenant Rendering, this term emphasizes that mercy itself becomes a public testimony to David's character and worthiness to rule.

word_study.meaning: Second person feminine singular of asah, 'to do, to make, to act.' Here paired with tov (good), indicating an action that produces goodness or benefit.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that goodness is something one *does*, not merely something one feels or intends. David's restraint is an action, a choice, a deed that constitutes genuine tov.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular Qal of sagar, meaning 'to shut, to close, to enclose, to hand over.' The root suggests entrapment or confinement—being shut in with no exit.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, the verb evokes the image of a gate closing around a prisoner. Saul was not merely defeated or outnumbered; he was entirely enclosed in David's hand, trapped, helpless. The theological weight: God actively 'shut' Saul into David's power, creating the circumstance for David's mercy.

word_study.meaning: lo ('not') + second person masculine singular Qal of harag ('to kill, to slay, to murder'). The negation emphasizes what did *not* happen against the expectation that it should have.
word_study.significance: The force of this phrase lies in its negation: it names the very thing David *could* have done but *did not*. It is an act of non-action that speaks louder than action. In ancient Near Eastern ethics, the restraint to kill an enemy when you have the power to do so is exceedingly rare and morally remarkable.

cross_references.connection: Samuel's pronouncement to Saul: 'The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.' Saul's confession here echoes the truth Samuel declared long ago—David is indeed the chosen one.
Jonathan speaks to David: 'Thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth.' Now Saul himself confirms what Jonathan already understood.

A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof.' David's wisdom in not using his military advantage mirrors the proverb's teaching about true power—it lies not in force but in discernment.

God's covenant promise to David: 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men; but my mercy shall not depart away from him.' The quality of mercy Saul recognizes in David is the same quality David will receive from God.

A very real picture of sacrifice and mercy: 'And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice.' David's restraint foreshadows the mercy that overcomes judgment in Christ.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, when a military opponent found an enemy at their mercy—trapped, defenseless, vulnerable—the expected course was execution. Mercy toward an enemy was so rare that it required explanation and often carried religious significance. The fact that Saul attributes his deliverance to the LORD rather than simply crediting David's compassion reflects the cultural assumption that such restraint required divine intervention. Saul's acknowledgment of David's *tov*—his goodness—was recognizing a quality that transcended normal human behavior in the warrior culture of Iron Age Levant. The cave encounter would have been understood by ancient readers not as a touching moment but as evidence of something supernatural at work in David's character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 27 presents a similar dynamic: the Lamanites, having pursued the Anti-Nephi-Lehies with deadly intent, witness their restraint and mercy (the Anti-Nephi-Lehies lay down their weapons and refuse to kill), and this non-resistance becomes a powerful testimony that moves the Lamanites toward repentance. Like David, the Anti-Nephi-Lehies demonstrate that true strength lies in the refusal to use violence, even when justified.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39–42 teaches the principle David embodies here: 'The rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven, and that the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness. That they may be conferred upon us, it is true; but when we undertake to cover our sins, or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition, or to exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness, behold, the heavens withdraw themselves; the Spirit of the Lord is grieved.' David's restraint, his refusal to exercise the power he possesses, is the very principle of righteous power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the aspirant covenants to avoid harming others and to live according to principles of mercy and justice. David's choice in the cave—to spare Saul's life despite the opportunity and justification for revenge—mirrors the covenantal commitment to mercy that transcends the natural man's impulse to retaliate.

commentary.christological_typology: David's merciful restraint when Saul is entirely in his power prefigures Christ's restraint toward His persecutors. Just as David did not use his power over Saul to destroy him, Christ possessed all power to call legions of angels to destroy those who crucified Him (Matthew 26:53), yet He refrained. The pattern is identical: absolute power coupled with absolute restraint, which becomes the highest testimony to divine character. David's mercy toward Saul reveals what kind of king he is; Christ's mercy toward His enemies reveals what kind of God He is.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites reflection on how we exercise power over others—whether in family dynamics, workplace relationships, or community leadership. The implicit teaching is that true strength is measured not by the power we wield but by our willingness to refrain from using it when justified. When you have the capacity to wound, shame, or destroy someone who has wronged you, the choice to forbear becomes a moral statement. Like David, we are called to 'show' our goodness not through retaliation but through demonstrated mercy that makes visible the Lord's work in our hearts.

text_kjv: For if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? wherefore the LORD reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day.

commentary.narrative: Saul moves from acknowledgment of David's mercy to blessing. His opening rhetorical question ('when a man finds his enemy, will he send him on his way unharmed?') is almost bitterly self-aware: Saul recognizes that what David just did violates the normal logic of survival and vengeance. In the world as Saul understands it, enemies are eliminated when the opportunity presents itself. Yet David did the unthinkable. The question itself is an indirect praise—Saul is saying, 'What you just did should not be possible; it contradicts everything I know about human nature.' This recognition opens Saul to pronounce a blessing: 'May the LORD repay you with good for what you have done for me today.'
commentary.narrative_cont: The blessing Saul speaks here is sincere and theologically weighted. He invokes the LORD as the one who will repay (*yeshallemekhah*), placing the fulfillment of David's reward in God's hands, not his own. This is significant because it suggests Saul understands that his own death may be imminent—he cannot repay David himself, so he commits David to God's care. The word *shalom*, which shares the same root as *yeshallemekhah* (repay/peace), adds theological depth: Saul is praying that God will bring David to a state of completeness, wholeness, and peace—even as David is currently a hunted fugitive with no safety, no kingdom, no stable home. The prayer is for David's ultimate restoration and flourishing.
commentary.narrative_cont2: Yet the narrative tension is profound. Saul's words are genuine—the text gives us no reason to doubt his sincerity in this moment. He truly means the blessing. But the reader already knows (and will soon see confirmed) that Saul will resume his pursuit. The text does not resolve this tension; it leaves it raw. This is one of Scripture's most honest portrayals of human nature: a man can be genuinely moved, can truly speak words of truth and goodness, can invoke God's blessing on his enemy, and then—driven by fear, pride, or desperation—return to his former destructive patterns. Saul is not lying; Saul is fractured.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular Qal of matza, 'to find, to encounter, to meet.' In this context, 'to come upon by chance or circumstance,' implying an unexpected encounter.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests serendipity or divine providence—not that enemies seek each other out, but that they 'find' each other through the working of Providence. Saul is acknowledging that their encounter in the cave was not mere chance.

word_study.meaning: Piel of shalach ('to send, to dispatch, to release') + 'in a good way/path.' The combination suggests not merely releasing someone but sending them away with blessing, protection, and good wishes.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes the completeness of David's mercy: he not only spared Saul's life but sent him away *unharmed*, on a good path, with his reputation intact. This is mercy beyond mere survival.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular Qal of shalam, meaning 'to repay, to reward, to recompense, to complete, to make whole.' The same root as shalom (peace) and Shelomoh (Solomon).
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, Saul's prayer for God to 'repay' David is simultaneously a prayer for David to be brought to shalom—wholeness, completeness, peace. This is not a transactional repayment but a restoration to a state of divine favor and security. The root's connection to both repayment and peace suggests that true reward is not material gain but the restoration of right relationship.

word_study.meaning: Feminine noun meaning 'goodness, that which is good, benefit, favor.' Used throughout 1 Samuel to describe moral quality and divine favor.
word_study.significance: The repetition of *tov* / *tovah* in verse 20 reinforces that David's action was good, and Saul's prayer is that God will repay goodness for goodness. This creates a moral equation: goodness deserves goodness as its return.

cross_references.connection: He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity; but he that soweth goodness shall reap mercy.' Saul recognizes that David has sown goodness and may expect to reap mercy from God in return.

Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.' David's response to Saul's murderous pursuit is to overcome it not with more violence but with goodness—the very principle Paul articulates to the Romans.

David will later declare: 'The LORD render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness.' David's own faith in God's ultimate justice shapes his willingness to leave Saul's fate in God's hands rather than take revenge.

For my love they are my adversaries; but I give myself unto prayer. And they have rewarded me evil for good.' The psalms often express the pain of doing good to those who repay with evil—a tension David knows intimately in his relationship with Saul.

Therefore, I say unto you, that ye shall forgive one another your trespasses; for verily I say unto you, he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord.' The Lord's modern covenant echoes the principle Saul articulates: forgiveness must precede blessing.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal practice, the blessing of one king upon another was not merely ceremonial; it was understood to carry power and to invoke divine sanction. Saul's blessing of David would have been heard by witnesses and recorded as a formal statement. In cultures where oral tradition was paramount and where words—especially words invoking God—carried performative power, Saul's blessing of David created a public record that worked against Saul's later attempts to kill David. The very words Saul speaks here will later be cited as evidence that he himself acknowledged David's worthiness and divine favor. Additionally, the practice of sparing one's enemy and pronouncing blessing upon him was associated in the ancient world with divine favor and prophetic insight—Saul's willingness to bless David (even as he fears him) suggests that something supernatural has broken through Saul's resistance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:12, Ammon reflects: 'I do not boast in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom; but behold, my joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I will rejoice in my God.' The joy Ammon describes comes from seeing former enemies (the Lamanites) converted—similar to how Saul's moment here contains both the pain of acknowledging his replacement and the grace of witnessing David's goodness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:9–10 teaches the covenant principle: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' Saul's blessing of David, spoken even as he fears David's rise, is a step toward this very forgiveness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the endowed member learns that the highest form of power is the power to bless—to invoke divine power on behalf of others. Saul, in his kingship, possesses the authority to bless, and his blessing of David becomes a moment where Saul's office works according to divine law rather than earthly fear.

commentary.christological_typology: Saul's blessing of David, the man who will replace him, prefigures the Father's blessing upon the Son. Just as Saul (the sitting king) blesses David (the future king), the Father blesses Jesus: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' (Matthew 3:17). The blessing does not negate Saul's current position but acknowledges a greater purpose and power at work. Similarly, the Father's blessing of Christ does not diminish the Father's authority but reveals the divine plan unfolding across generations.
commentary.application: This verse calls modern disciples to bless those whom they fear or oppose. It invites the question: Can I genuinely pray for someone's welfare even when I feel threatened by them? Saul's prayer—'May the LORD repay you with good'—models the mature faith that entrusts both enemies and the future to God's hands. In families, workplaces, and faith communities, there are moments when someone's rise threatens our position, security, or pride. The spiritual maturity Saul displays here (however briefly) is the capacity to speak blessing across that tension, to invoke God's goodness upon someone whose success means our own diminishment. This is the charity that 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (1 Corinthians 13:6).

text_kjv: And now, behold, I know well that thou shalt surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in thine hand.

commentary.narrative: Saul's confession reaches its apex: 'I know that you will certainly be king.' This is not speculation, hope, or fear—it is a statement of absolute certainty. Saul uses the emphatic infinitive absolute construction (*malokh timlokh*, 'you will certainly reign'), the same grammatical intensifier that God Himself employs when speaking with finality (as in Genesis 2:17, *mot tamut*, 'you will surely die'). By adopting this divine linguistic pattern, Saul is not merely sharing an opinion but acknowledging what he experiences as divinely determined inevitability. The kingdom will not merely pass to David; it will be *established* in his hand (*qamah beyadekha mamlekhet Yisra'el*), using the verb *qum* ('to rise, to stand, to endure'), which implies permanence and stability—the opposite of Saul's own dynasty, which will not endure.
commentary.narrative_cont: This confession is staggering precisely because Saul makes it about his own succession. He is not speaking of David in general terms—'a worthy man,' 'a good warrior'—but specifically about David as *king of Israel*. Saul is sitting king, and he is acknowledging that David will be the next king. This echoes what Samuel pronounced in chapter 15 ('The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou') and what Jonathan acknowledged in chapter 23 ('Thou shalt be king over Israel, and I will be next unto thee; and even my father Saul knoweth this'). Now Saul himself, the man most motivated to deny this truth and most threatened by it, joins the chorus. The convergence is astonishing: Samuel, Jonathan, and now Saul all speak the same truth that David will replace Saul's line.
commentary.narrative_cont2: Yet the reader must hold a paradox: this is the most honest and spiritually clear moment Saul has had since his rejection in chapter 15, and simultaneously it is meaningless to his behavior. Saul knows that David will be king. Saul has just blessed David and acknowledged his goodness. And Saul will, within a few chapters, return to his campaign to kill David. Knowledge and action, confession and behavior, are radically disconnected in Saul's soul. This is the tragedy of Saul: he is not ignorant or deceived; he knows the truth. He is simply unable to live according to what he knows. He is divided against himself, and no amount of spiritual insight can heal that division because the root problem is his refusal to submit to God's will.

word_study.meaning: First person singular Qal of yada, meaning 'to know, to understand, to become aware.' The Qal (simple) form emphasizes direct, immediate knowledge rather than abstract understanding.
word_study.significance: Saul is not theorizing; he is declaring what he directly knows. The verb suggests revelation, not mere inference—Saul has come to know this truth through lived experience and perhaps divine disclosure.

word_study.meaning: Infinitive absolute (malokh) + finite verb (timlokh), both from melek ('to reign, to be king'). The infinitive absolute construction with a finite verb of the same root creates emphatic intensification—literally 'reigning you will reign' or 'certainly you will be king.'
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, this is the same grammatical construction God uses when pronouncing divine judgment or certainty. By adopting this pattern, Saul speaks as though channeling prophetic certainty. The effect is to make the statement carry the weight of divine determination rather than human prediction.

word_study.meaning: Third person feminine singular Qal of qum, meaning 'to rise, to stand, to be established, to endure.' The feminine form agrees with the feminine noun 'kingdom' (mamlekhet).
word_study.significance: The verb suggests permanence and stability. David's kingdom will not be temporary or fragile like Saul's; it will rise, stand firm, and endure. The contrast is implicit: Saul's kingdom is falling (*naphal*), while David's will be established (*qum*).

word_study.meaning: Feminine noun meaning 'kingdom, realm, dominion, the sphere of a king's rule.' In 1 Samuel, the mamlekhet Yisra'el is the unified kingdom of all twelve tribes under a single monarch.
word_study.significance: Saul is acknowledging that not merely a region or tribe but the entire kingdom of Israel—the institution he currently holds—will pass to David. This is total, unreserved acknowledgment of successor.

word_study.meaning: Preposition be ('in') + noun yad ('hand'). The 'hand' in Hebrew idiom represents power, authority, control, agency. To put something in someone's hand is to give them authority over it.
word_study.significance: The phrase echoes verse 19, where Saul was 'in David's hand'—delivered and helpless. Now Saul acknowledges that the kingdom itself will be placed in David's hand—delivered to him by God, with authority and power. The symmetry is perfect: just as Saul was in David's hand in the cave and David showed mercy, the kingdom will be in David's hand and the dynasty will endure.

cross_references.connection: Samuel to Saul: 'The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.' Saul's confession here is his acknowledgment of what Samuel declared irrevocably in his rejection as king.

Jonathan to David: 'Thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth.' Jonathan reveals that Saul already knows the truth that Saul now openly confesses.

God's covenant to David: 'And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.' David's dynasty will indeed be established, though not in the way Saul currently envisions—through a succession of kings, not merely David's individual reign.

I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations.' The psalmist celebrates the eternal establishment of David's house, which Saul here acknowledges will surpass his own.

And I said unto them that it was the word of the Lord; and he hath power over all things whatsoever he will for the fulfillment of his words.' The principle that God's word determines future events, which Saul is now acknowledging in his own case.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, a reigning king would rarely (if ever) publicly acknowledge that his own dynasty would not continue. Such acknowledgment could embolden rivals, demoralize supporters, and destabilize the realm. For Saul to speak this confession aloud—even if only to David—was politically suicidal. Yet the historical record shows that Saul did indeed lose the kingdom, his sons did not inherit it (despite his hopes in verse 22), and David did establish a dynasty that lasted for centuries. The ancient reader, knowing the outcome, would understand Saul's confession as a moment of genuine prophetic clarity breaking through his resistance—a moment where Saul sees truth he has been denying and speaks it aloud. The fact that Saul cannot sustain this clarity and will return to his former pursuits makes the narrative even more tragic: the man glimpses the inevitable and then chooses to struggle against it anyway.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 12:2–3, the text describes a pattern of human nature: 'And thus we can behold how false, and also the unsteadiness of the hearts of the children of men; for there is nothing that is sure save it be God. Behold, he changes the hearts of men; he allureth them to repentance and to righteousness.' Saul's heart has been momentarily changed by the encounter in the cave—he sees truth—but will this change endure? The Book of Mormon teaches that lasting change requires covenantal commitment to God, which Saul has not made.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:29–30 addresses this very dynamic: 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' Saul's problem is precisely that he cannot relinquish authority, even when he knows it is passing from him. Knowledge of truth is not sufficient without willingness to surrender control.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the ordinances teach that progression comes through acceptance and submission to God's law and timing. Saul's confession of truth (verse 21) without willingness to submit (which verses 23-28 will show) exemplifies the tragedy of knowing doctrine but refusing to live it. The temple path requires both knowledge and covenant action.

commentary.christological_typology: Saul's acknowledgment that David will be king parallels the recognition of Christ in the Gospels. Just as Saul knows with certainty that David will reign, the demons in the Gospels recognize Jesus: 'Thou art the Son of God' (Luke 4:41). Recognition of truth does not equal acceptance or submission. The Devil himself knows that Jesus is the Son of God, yet this knowledge does not lead to repentance. Similarly, Saul's knowledge that David will be king does not lead him to cease his pursuit. In both cases, correct doctrine and genuine knowledge fail to produce righteousness when they are not paired with covenant submission.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse invites uncomfortable self-examination: Do I truly know that God's will is being accomplished in my life, in my family, in the world, even when it contradicts my preferences or threatens my plans? Knowledge and submission are not the same. Saul knows the truth. The question is whether he will accept it. In our own lives, we may 'know' many truths—that God is in control, that His plan is unfolding, that His kingdom will succeed, that pride and resistance are futile—yet our actions may reveal that we have not truly surrendered to that knowledge. This verse is a call to examine the gap between what we profess to know and how we actually live. Do our decisions reflect genuine faith in God's plan, or are we like Saul, knowing the outcome while fighting against it?

text_kjv: Swear now therefore unto me by the LORD, that thou wilt not cut off my seed after me, and that thou wilt not destroy my name out of my father's house.

commentary.narrative: Saul's final request flows naturally from his acknowledgment: if David will be king after him, then Saul's deepest concern is dynastic survival. Having confessed that David will inherit the throne, Saul now asks David for a binding oath to preserve Saul's descendants and name. The request is entirely rational within ancient Near Eastern practice. A new king, especially one who had been hunted and opposed by his predecessor, would typically consolidate power by eliminating all potential rivals from the previous dynasty—this actually happened repeatedly in the northern kingdom (see 1 Kings 15:29, 16:11, 2 Kings 10:17). Saul's fear was not paranoid but historically grounded. The oath he requests is *hashbe'ah li ba-Adonai*, 'swear to me by the LORD'—the most solemn binding commitment available, invoking God as witness and guarantor.
commentary.narrative_cont: Saul's two concerns are expressed with the harshest verbs available: *takhrit et zar'i* ('you will not cut off my seed') and *tashmid et shemi* ('you will not wipe out my name'). The verb *karat* is the 'covenant-cutting' word, but here it means to exterminate, to sever completely. The verb *shamad* means to annihilate, to destroy utterly. Together, they express the fear of total erasure. In the ancient world, to cut off a man's seed was to eliminate his descendants; to wipe out his name was to erase him from human memory and genealogical record. A man without descendants and without a remembered name had, in effect, never existed. Saul asks David to grant what David just demonstrated: merciful restraint even when one has the power to destroy. Saul recognizes that David spared his body in the cave; now he asks David to spare his dynasty after his death.
commentary.narrative_cont2: This request reveals Saul's ultimate fear beneath his fear of David: the fear of non-existence. It is not merely death that terrifies Saul but the extinction of his name and seed, the obliteration of any trace that he ever ruled, ever mattered. This is a deeply human fear, and it makes Saul sympathetic even in his decline. Yet it also reveals a fundamental failure of faith: Saul seeks security in David's oath rather than in God's covenant. He has acknowledged that the kingdom belongs to David by divine determination (verse 21), yet he asks David (not God) for protection. The narrative leaves this tension unresolved. David will swear the oath (as we learn from the next verses), and David will honor it (2 Samuel 9 confirms his covenant with Jonathan's house), but the path to that honor will be complicated by other events (2 Samuel 21).

word_study.meaning: Hiphil imperative of shaba, meaning 'to swear, to take an oath.' The Hiphil causative form here is second person masculine singular: 'cause yourself to swear' or 'swear yourself.'
word_study.significance: The verb carries legal and covenantal weight. To swear is not merely to promise but to invoke God as witness and to bind oneself by divine sanction. Breaking a swear oath was understood to invite divine punishment.

word_study.meaning: Preposition be + divine name Yahweh (rendered as 'LORD' in KJV). To swear 'by the LORD' is to invoke God's name as the binding power of the oath.
word_study.significance: The oath's validity rests not on David's authority but on God's. Saul is asking David to bind himself before God, making the oath a three-party covenant between Saul, David, and the LORD. This is the most serious form of commitment in ancient Israel.

word_study.meaning: Second person masculine singular future of karat, meaning 'to cut, to cut off, to sever, to exterminate.' The root 'covenant-cutting' (karit) comes from the same verb, but here it means to eliminate or destroy completely.
word_study.significance: The verb *karat* is used throughout 1 Samuel when discussing the end of Saul's dynasty (14:39, 15:28). Saul is asking David not to use the very power that the narrative already attributes to David as Saul's successor. The irony is profound: Saul fears that David will do what is historically normal for a new king to do.

word_study.meaning: Noun 'seed, offspring, descendants, progeny.' Used throughout the Bible to refer to biological and covenantal lineage (as in 'seed of Abraham').
word_study.significance: The term carries both biological meaning (Saul's actual descendants) and covenantal meaning (the continuation of Saul's line as a dynasty). Saul is asking for both literal survival (his grandchildren) and institutional continuation (his house remaining among the great families of Israel).

word_study.meaning: Second person masculine singular future of shamad, meaning 'to destroy, to annihilate, to wipe out, to exterminate completely.' Often used for the total destruction of peoples or cities.
word_study.significance: The term is even more comprehensive than *karat*. While *karat* focuses on cutting off descendants, *shamad* focuses on erasing from existence entirely. Combined with the next phrase, it emphasizes total annihilation.

word_study.meaning: Noun 'name, reputation, fame, memorial.' In Hebrew thought, a man's 'name' is his reputation, his place in collective memory, his legacy.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern culture, to have one's name remembered was to maintain a form of existence even after death. To have one's name 'blotted out' was considered a fate worse than death—it was total obliteration. Saul is asking David to preserve his memorial, his place in history, his name among the people.

word_study.meaning: Noun construction: 'house [dynasty] of my father.' The 'house' (bet) is the dynasty or clan, the extended family structure that perpetuates identity and inheritance.
word_study.significance: The term is covenantal in resonance. 'House of David' becomes a title for the dynasty; similarly, 'House of Saul' was the dynasty that Saul founded. To preserve one's father's house is to ensure that the family line continues to be recognized as a significant people in the nation.

cross_references.connection: David honors the oath he swears here, bringing Mephibosheth (Jonathan's son, Saul's grandson) to the royal table and restoring his father's land. David's covenantal integrity is demonstrated in his treatment of Saul's house generations later.

Solomon executes Joab at David's deathbed instructions because Joab had murdered Abner and Amasa. This shows that the securing of dynasty sometimes requires eliminating rivals—precisely what Saul fears David will do to his house. Yet David's oath protects Saul's descendants from this fate.

Abimelech asks Abraham to swear by God that Abraham will not deal falsely with him: 'Now therefore swear unto me here by God.' The parallel pattern of requesting a binding oath to prevent future harm from a more powerful party.

A famine comes upon David's house because Saul had broken covenant with the Gibeonites. David then executes seven of Saul's descendants to make atonement, which complicates (though does not violate) his earlier oath to preserve Saul's house. This shows how covenantal promises can be tested by intervening events.

Let his posterity be cut off; and in the generation following let their name be blotted out.' The psalmist's curse mirrors Saul's fear—that posterity will be cut off and name blotted out. Saul's request addresses exactly this fear.

All Israel stoned [Achan], and burned them with fire after they had stoned them with stones. And they raised over him a great heap of stones unto this day.' The raising of a memorial heap ensures that a name is remembered in Israel—the opposite of what Saul fears.

commentary.historical_context: Saul's request reflects actual ancient Near Eastern practice. When a new dynasty took power, eliminating the previous royal family was standard policy. The pattern is explicitly documented in 1 Kings 15:29 (Baasha kills all the house of Jeroboam), 16:11 (Zimri kills all the house of Baasha), and 2 Kings 10:17 (Jehu kills all the house of Ahab). The practice was so common that a new king who *did not* eliminate his predecessor's family would be unusual. Saul's fear, then, was not based on paranoia but on historical reality. His request for David's oath was his only protection against a practice that had become dynastic tradition in northern Israel. Additionally, in ancient Near Eastern understanding, the preservation of a name was understood as a form of immortality. To have one's name remembered in genealogy, on monuments, or in oral tradition was to achieve a kind of afterlife. Saul's concern to preserve his name was not vanity but a reflection of cultural values about memorial and legacy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 2:30–31, King Benjamin addresses the succession: 'And moreover, I say unto you that there shall be no disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there have hitherto been; for ye have disputed over the interpretation of all the scriptures; but, behold, ye ought to take upon you the name of Christ.' Unlike Saul's anxiety about preserving his own name, King Benjamin teaches that the true name to be preserved is the name of Christ. The contrast is instructive: Saul seeks preservation of his personal name; Benjamin directs his people to take upon them Christ's name.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 130:14–15 teaches: 'Joseph Smith received many revelations, but he did not receive a fulness at any one time. But he received a little here and a little there, having line upon line and precept upon precept, here a little and there a little.' The covenant God makes with David's house (which David will honor through his oath) follows the pattern of God's covenant making: binding, eternal, and carried out over generations. David's oath, like God's covenants, extends beyond David's lifetime to protect his posterity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, one covenants not only for oneself but with an eye toward posterity and generational blessing. Saul's concern for his descendants reflects this theological principle—that faithfulness or unfaithfulness has consequences for future generations. David's willingness to swear an oath that protects Saul's house is a form of the merciful stewardship taught in the temple: those with power are entrusted to use it righteously toward others, even enemies.

commentary.christological_typology: Saul's request for David to spare his descendants and preserve his name foreshadows the prayer of all humanity to God through Christ. Just as Saul appeals to David's mercy to preserve his house, all people appeal to God through Christ's mercy to preserve us eternally. In Romans 6:9, Paul teaches that 'Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more'; through Christ, the righteous achieve eternal name and seed—spiritual descendants who carry forward the covenant. Where Saul fears extinction, those who come to Christ through His covenant receive eternal continuation. The mercy David shows Saul prefigures the mercy Christ shows to all who accept His covenant.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse raises important questions about mercy, legacy, and the use of power. If you ever occupy a position where you have authority over someone who has opposed you, will you remember Saul's fear and Saul's request? Will you extend the mercy that spares not just the body but the legacy, the reputation, the family line? David's willingness to swear this oath shows maturity that Saul, despite his confession, has not achieved—Saul cannot give up his anxiety even after he has acknowledged the inevitability of David's reign. For modern members, this is a call to a deeper release: not just intellectual acknowledgment of God's will, but emotional and behavioral surrender that expresses itself in generosity toward those we fear. The willingness to bless one's successor, to swear that their children will not be harmed, to protect the family name of one who opposed you—this is covenant-level righteousness. Where in your life do you need to make this transition from mere knowledge to genuine surrender and generosity?

text_kjv: And Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah. And David arose, and went down to the wilderness of Paran.

commentary.narrative:
Samuel's death marks the end of an era. The narrative announces it with stark brevity—three verbs, and the judge who shaped Israel's transition to monarchy is gone. The gathering of all Israel and their formal lamentation (safad, the ritualized beating of the breast) signals Samuel's singular importance: he was the last figure to unite the fractured tribes before the monarchy splintered them into competing interests. The burial in his house at Ramah echoes the opening of his own story (1:19); Ramah was his birthplace and family seat, and now it becomes his tomb—a full circle of life contained within one place.

The immediate shift to David is deliberate: "And David arose, and went down." The Hebrew verb qum (to rise, to stand up) paired with yarad (to go down) signals transition and movement. David descends into the wilderness of Paran, the vast desert region in the northern Sinai, far from Saul's reach and far from the centers of power. The reader encounters a striking irony: Samuel has just been buried, the spiritual anchor of Israel gone, while David—the Lord's chosen future king—is isolated in the wilderness, stripped of authority, hunted by a paranoid monarch. The old order is dead; the new order is not yet born. David is in the liminal space between promise and fulfillment.

word_study.meaning: To mourn formally; to beat the breast or tear garments in ritualized grief; implies communal, official mourning rather than private sorrow
word_study.significance: The use of safad (rather than bakah, simply 'to weep') indicates that Samuel's death triggered formal national lamentation—an institutional grief. This verb appears in prophetic contexts when entire nations mourn collective loss (Jeremiah 4:8). Samuel's death is not a private family tragedy but a covenant-level event.

word_study.meaning: To stand up, rise up, get up; carries connotations of initiative, readiness, and purposeful action; in narrative contexts often signals a turning point or new phase
word_study.significance: The pairing of qum ('David arose') with Samuel's death is theological—David's rising corresponds to Samuel's falling. The verb qum will appear repeatedly in covenant narrative when a leader is raised up for God's purposes (cf. Judges 2:16, 3:9). David's qum here is not casual movement but purposeful emergence as the figure who will fill the void Samuel leaves.

word_study.meaning: Desert, wilderness; in biblical narrative, a place of testing, purification, divine encounter, and preparation for covenant service
word_study.significance: The wilderness is not merely geography but theological space. Israel wandered the midbar for forty years (Exodus). Moses encountered God in the midbar. David's descent into Paran places him in the liminal zone where God refines His servants. The Covenant Rendering notes that some manuscripts read 'Maon' (closer to the action that follows) rather than 'Paran,' but the Masoretic 'Paran' emphasizes David's extreme isolation—he is as distant from political power as possible while remaining in the land.

cross_references.connection: Samuel's establishment as a prophet 'whom all Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew'—his death therefore represents the loss of a figure known and trusted across the entire nation.
Samuel's role as judge who 'judged Israel all the days of his life'—his death closes that chapter of leadership.
The gathering and formal mourning parallels Israel's mourning for Moses—both mark the death of a transformative leader who held the nation together.
David's entrance into wilderness follows the pattern of the Psalmist's valley of the shadow of death—yet God prepares a table before him, even in the presence of enemies.
Samuel anointed David in the previous narrative; his death occurs after David has been marked for kingship, leaving David to navigate the gap between promise and throne.

commentary.historical_context: Samuel's death represents a historical and religious turning point in Israel. The period of the judges was ending; Samuel was the last judge who held genuine authority over all twelve tribes. After his death, that unity fractured. Ramah, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, was Samuel's administrative and spiritual center. The mention of burial 'in his house' reflects ancient Near Eastern practice: family tombs on household property were common among the wealthy. The wilderness of Paran (modern-day Negev/Sinai region) was sparsely inhabited—David's retreat there suggests he was avoiding Saul's agents while maintaining some connection to the southern Judahite territories where his own tribe held influence. The timing is significant: David is now fully exposed. Without Samuel's prophetic authority to legitimate him, without Saul's patronage (long since revoked), David is a fugitive dependent on maintaining agreements with local chieftains like Nabal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The wilderness as a place of preparation and testing appears throughout the Book of Mormon: Nephi's family flees into the wilderness (1 Nephi 2); Alma and his followers hide in the wilderness and are refined through persecution (Mosiah 24); the Lamanites who repent must separate from their civilization and wander (Alma 47-48). David's descent into Paran parallels these passages: the wilderness strips away false power and prepares leaders for covenant service.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 136:31 describes the condition of those who follow the Lord as sometimes requiring them to be 'cast out and despised'—yet this humiliation becomes preparation for exaltation. David's exile in the wilderness (verse 1) is precisely this pattern: he is rejected, isolated, homeless, yet being prepared for kingship. The narrative arc of 1 Samuel 17-26 shows David becoming progressively more 'despised' by Saul while becoming more beloved to the people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Samuel's death and burial mark the end of the sanctuary period centered on the tabernacle at Ramah and Shiloh. David will eventually establish a new sanctuary at Jerusalem. The transition from Samuel to David parallels the transition from the tabernacle-centered priesthood to the Davidic covenant—both involve a shift in how God's presence dwells with Israel and who mediates covenant access.

commentary.christological_typology: David's wilderness experience foreshadows Christ's wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:1-11). Both figures are marked for kingship, both experience rejection and isolation, both are tested in the wilderness. Both emerge from the wilderness prepared for their covenant work. Samuel's death leaves a vacuum in Israel's spiritual leadership; David's wilderness sojourn prepares him to fill that gap. Similarly, Christ's wilderness testing prepares Him to fill the ultimate gap between fallen humanity and a holy God.
commentary.application: This verse marks a threshold in David's life and invites modern readers to recognize their own wilderness seasons. The death of one chapter—whether literal, relational, or professional—often precedes the beginning of the next. When trusted authorities or familiar structures collapse, we may find ourselves in a 'wilderness of Paran,' isolated and unclear about the future. Yet the narrative teaches that the wilderness is not punishment but preparation. David's isolation in Paran is not the end of his story; it is the crucible in which he becomes the leader Israel needs. For covenant members, this suggests that periods of testing, humbling, and seeming exile from cultural power are often the Lord's way of preparing us for unexpected service. The question is not 'Why am I in the wilderness?' but 'What is God teaching me here?'

text_kjv: And there was a man in Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel; and the man was very great, and he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats: and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.

commentary.narrative:
The scene shifts abruptly from David's wilderness exile to the household of a man of great wealth. Nabal lives in Maon (a town in the hill country south of Hebron) but conducts his business in Carmel (not Mount Carmel in the north, but a town closer to his estate, about 10 miles south of Hebron). The narrator emphasizes his wealth with specificity: three thousand sheep and a thousand goats—an enormous flock by ancient standards, suggesting Nabal's herds numbered around four thousand animals in total. This would make him one of the wealthiest landowners in Judah.

The timing is crucial: he is shearing his sheep, and sheep-shearing was far more than a utilitarian task. It was a festival season—the ancient equivalent of harvest celebration. Shearing occurred in spring when the wool was abundant, and it was an occasion marked by feasting, celebration, and conspicuous generosity. The wealthy were expected to provide food and drink for workers, neighbors, and those who had supported their enterprises over the preceding year. The narrator thus establishes the narrative's first tension: here is a man at the moment when his wealth is most evident and his obligations to extend generosity are culturally highest. Into this scene, David will soon send his men with a request that should be easily granted.

word_study.meaning: Great, large, mighty; in the context of a person, refers primarily to wealth, power, and social standing rather than moral virtue or character
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that gadol here is about material magnitude, not moral greatness. The word will take on ironic weight in verse 3, where Nabal is great in possessions but shown to be small in character. The same Hebrew word describes God's greatness (Psalm 104:1), the greatness of David's kingdom (2 Samuel 5:10), and the greatness of Nabal's flocks. The juxtaposition is jarring: one can be gadol (great) in the world's accounting and yet spiritually and morally diminished.

word_study.meaning: To shear, to cut (wool from sheep); in narrative context, the seasonal activity that triggers celebration and hospitality
word_study.significance: Gazaz signals the harvest moment in pastoral economy. The root appears in contexts of abundance and provision (Genesis 38:12, where Judah goes to his sheepshearers). In David's case, the shearing season becomes the moment when his claim for protection-compensation should be honored. The verb frames Nabal not as a threat but as a man at his moment of plenty.

word_study.meaning: Work, deed, possession, enterprise; refers to the productive operations or holdings of a household
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'business,' which captures the sense that Nabal's ma'aseh in Carmel is an active enterprise, not merely land he owns. His whole economic operation is centered there. The word ma'aseh (literally 'work') appears throughout the narrative to describe human action and its moral weight. In verse 3, Nabal will be condemned for 'evil deeds' (ra ma'alalim)—his actions produce harm. Here, his ma'aseh is simply described factually, but the narrative is setting up the contrast between what Nabal has built and what his character actually is.

cross_references.connection: Nabal's own servants later testify that David's men 'were a wall unto us both by night and day' while protecting the flocks—establishing that David's request in verse 5 is based on actual service rendered.
Judah goes to his sheepshearers in Timnah, a setting of festivity and abundance—the cultural context that makes sheep-shearing a natural occasion for hospitality and blessing.
The royal court's daily provisions (including specific numbers of animals) illustrate the scale of wealth that great landholders possessed—Nabal's four thousand animals places him among the elite.
Job's opening description parallels Nabal's: both are men of 'very great' possessions (gadol me'od), yet the narrative will immediately test their character—wealth does not guarantee righteousness.

Later in the narrative, David will claim to have preserved Nabal's flocks from Amalekite raids (though this verse makes no such claim)—David's later self-justification depends on the cultural assumption that protecting flocks obligates repayment.

commentary.historical_context: Maon and Carmel were both towns in the Judahite hill country, roughly 20-30 miles south of Jerusalem. Archaeological surveys suggest the hill country south of Hebron was settled by small landholding communities; Nabal's scale of operation would place him among the wealthiest 1-2% of the population. Three thousand sheep and a thousand goats is not hyperbole—such flocks are documented in ancient Near Eastern records. Sheep-shearing was indeed a festive occasion. Ancient Ugaritic and Egyptian texts describe sheepshearing celebrations with feasting and gift-giving. The social expectation was that during this season of abundance, a wealthy man would dispense hospitality broadly—to workers, to the poor, to clients and allies. The failure to do so would mark a man as stingy, anti-social, and in violation of tribal customs. David's later attack on Nabal (verse 13) and Nabal's subsequent death (verse 37-38) both occur within the framework of this cultural expectation: Nabal has violated a sacred custom, and the narrative audience would understand the judgment as consonant with justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The contrast between material wealth and spiritual poverty appears in the Book of Mormon's description of the rich Nephites who have become 'lifted up in the pride of their eyes' (Helaman 6:35, 3 Nephi 6:14-15). Nabal's gadol status (great wealth) parallels the prideful Nephite elite who trust in riches rather than in God's covenants. Mormon's editorial voice condemns those who use wealth to dominate rather than serve—precisely Nabal's disposition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:39 warns that 'it is not given that one man should possess that which is above another, wherefore the world lieth in sin.' Nabal's hoarding of his wealth during the very season when generosity is expected violates this principle. His four thousand animals in a land where David's men lack sustenance embodies the inequality D&C condemns.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of consecration in the temple covenant teaches that abundance is stewardship, not ownership. Nabal treats his possessions as his own to withhold; a covenant-keeping perspective would recognize that his herds exist under God's provision and carry obligations to the community. His failure to share at the shearing season violates the spirit of consecration.

commentary.christological_typology: Nabal's refusal to recognize David's worth or to offer hospitality parallels the world's rejection of Christ. Just as Nabal looks at David and sees only a wilderness fugitive (not recognizing his chosen status), the religious and political authorities of Christ's time failed to recognize His kingship. The shearing season becomes a type of the 'time appointed'—the kairos moment when the world's wealth is most evident and generosity is most expected, yet both Nabal and the world-system withhold blessing from the one they should honor.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with the uncomfortable question: Do we recognize our wealth as abundance from God's hand, and do we act accordingly? Nabal is described neutrally here—he is simply rich, and it is simply shearing season. But the narrative is preparing us to judge his response. For contemporary covenant members, the principle is clear: abundance creates obligation. A successful career, a healthy family, financial surplus—these are not gifts to hoard but stewardships to manage with generosity. The 'shearing seasons' in our lives (times of plenty, promotions, inheritances, increased income) are precisely the moments when God tests whether we will recognize our debts to family, community, and those who have served us. Nabal's failure to do so will cost him everything; his example warns us not to confuse gadol (great wealth) with gadol character (genuine greatness).

text_kjv: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.

commentary.narrative:
The narrator paints the marriage as a study in radical opposites. Nabal and Abigail are not two people growing together; they are forces in opposition, held together by marriage but fundamentally mismatched. Abigail is described with terms of moral and intellectual virtue: tovat-sekhel (good understanding, shrewd discernment) and yefat to'ar (beautiful in appearance). The word sekhel does not mean mere intelligence; it is practical wisdom, the ability to read a situation, perceive consequences, and act with discretion. It is the quality that allows someone to navigate complex social terrain. Abigail possesses it; Nabal lacks it entirely.

Nabal, by contrast, is qashah (hard, harsh, intractable) and ra ma'alalim (evil in his dealings, destructive in his habitual actions). The verb ra describes not a single moral lapse but a pattern—his dealings, his way of conducting business and relationships, produce harm. The word ma'alalim (from the root alal, 'to do, to act') emphasizes that this is who he is functionally; his actions embody his character. The narrator then adds a genealogical note: 'He was of the house of Caleb.' This is pointed irony. Caleb—the faithful scout who alone with Joshua trusted God at Kadesh-barnea, who received a blessing to possess the hill country—this Caleb's descendant has become a man whose very name means 'fool.'

The Covenant Rendering notes that Naval (Nabal) is almost certainly not a birth name but a label, a judgment pronounced on him by the community. By verse 25, Abigail will make this theology explicit when she says, 'As his name is, so is he: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him.' The narrator is not being unkind; he is describing the outcome of character. Nabal has become his name.

word_study.meaning: Fool, senseless one; not intellectual stupidity but moral and social recklessness; one who refuses to recognize obligations to God or community; the fool who says in his heart, 'There is no God' (Psalm 14:1)
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that naval denotes not low IQ but practical rejection of covenant order. Nabal's foolishness will be on display in verse 10-11: he will refuse to acknowledge David's service, will reject the implicit covenant of mutuality that binds the community together. Calling him 'Nabal' is the narrator's way of rendering judgment: this man has become a fool by his refusal to honor obligations and relationships. The same word appears in Proverbs repeatedly (1:7, 10:1, 15:20) to describe those who despise wisdom and reject instruction—a category of person structurally opposed to the wise (hakham).

word_study.meaning: Good sense, practical discernment, shrewd judgment; sekhel is not abstract intelligence but the ability to perceive social and practical realities and act wisely within them
word_study.significance: Sekhel appears in wisdom literature (Proverbs 11:12, 14:29) to describe the quality that allows a person to navigate life successfully—to read situations, anticipate consequences, and choose wisely. Abigail's possession of this quality will become clear in verse 23-31, where she quickly grasps David's emotional state, the danger her household faces, and the exact right words to deflect him from violence. She has sekhel; Nabal lacks it entirely.

word_study.meaning: Hard, harsh, severe, difficult, stubborn; describes both physical hardness and emotional/relational hardness; intractability
word_study.significance: Qashah appears in descriptions of Pharaoh (hardened heart), of Job's affliction (hard skin), of unresponsive people. It suggests not mere gruffness but a fundamental resistance to empathy, negotiation, or change. Nabal is qashah—you cannot reach him, appeal to him, or move him. He is fixed in his refusal.

word_study.term_english: evil in his doings / destructive dealings
word_study.meaning: Evil of deeds/dealings; ra (evil, harm) paired with ma'alalim (habitual actions, dealings); refers not to a single bad act but to a pattern of destructive conduct
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice to render this as 'destructive in his dealings' captures the ongoing, relational harm Nabal causes. The same phrase appears in prophetic indictment (Jeremiah 4:4, Micah 3:4) to describe Israel's persistent unfaithfulness. Nabal's evil is not momentary but structural—it is how he conducts himself habitually.

word_study.meaning: Of the clan/family of Caleb; refers to descent from Caleb son of Jephunneh, one of the two faithful scouts
word_study.significance: The genealogical reference is ironic and pointed. Caleb was 'wholly followed the Lord' (Numbers 14:24) and received a covenant blessing to inherit Hebron and the hill country. His clan became one of the most honored lineages in Judah. That a descendant of Caleb has become 'Nabal' (a fool) represents a failure to inherit the spiritual legacy of the ancestor—and foreshadows that Abigail, marrying into the Calebite line, will recover something of Caleb's faithful character in her actions.

cross_references.connection: The opening of this psalm—'The fool (naval) hath said in his heart, There is no God'—defines the category Nabal embodies: one who refuses to acknowledge the order God has established.
Abigail will say of Nabal: 'As his name is, so is he: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him'—making the theology of the name explicit.
Caleb is blessed for his faithfulness: 'He wholly followed the Lord.' His lineage becomes distinguished. Nabal's refusal to honor covenant obligation is a repudiation of Caleb's legacy.
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding (sekhel); he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly'—Abigail's sekhel contrasts with Nabal's reactiveness and hardness.

The narrative's judgment on Nabal: when he learns what he did, 'his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And it came to pass about ten days after, that the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.' The fool's hardness (qashah) becomes literal: stone. The man of destructive dealings (ra ma'alalim) is destroyed.

commentary.historical_context: The genealogical reference to Caleb places this narrative within a specific tribal and historical context. Caleb's clan held the Hebron region and surrounding hill country (Joshua 14:13-15). The fact that Nabal is 'of the house of Caleb' means he belongs to Judah's most prestigious lineage. This raises his fall even higher—he is not a nobody but a man of distinguished family who has squandered the covenant heritage. The description of Abigail as 'beautiful' (yefat to'ar) is not merely aesthetic; in the ancient context, it suggests a woman of value who could have married advantageously. That she is married to Nabal suggests either an arranged marriage that went poorly or that she married down (or that Nabal married above his character). The contrast between Nabal's harsh character and Abigail's wisdom and beauty sets up the narrative's greatest tension: a marriage of radical incompatibility, held together only by law, about to be tested by David's arrival.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon presents several figures who bear names or reputations that become self-fulfilling judgments. The description of Nabal as 'foolish' (naval) parallels Mormon's condemnation of the wicked among both Nephites and Lamanites who 'believed not in the power of God' (Alma 32:27). Abigail's sekhel—practical discernment about covenant realities—echoes the quality that allows Alma to navigate through periods of apostasy and unbelief (Alma 5:43, 12:1-3).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39 warns against the 'unrighteous dominion' that Nabal embodies: 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' Nabal's wealth gives him authority; his hardness and destructive dealings show how he exercises it. The passage teaches that such dominion cannot be sustained—'It is the only principle on which God pity us.' Nabal's refusal to govern with kindness brings judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The contrast between Nabal and Abigail reflects the temple covenant's emphasis on wisdom and charity. Abigail's sekhel (discernment) and her later actions (verse 23-31) embody the covenant woman's role as one who preserves household and brings peace through wisdom. Nabal's hardness and refusal to honor covenant obligation represent the rejection of the order the temple teaches.

commentary.christological_typology: Abigail's character and role foreshadow the Bride of Christ—the one who possesses wisdom (sekhel), beauty (yefat to'ar), and who acts to reconcile, to prevent bloodshed, and to make peace where her husband (or the world system) refuses. Her intervention on behalf of Nabal's household (though Nabal does not deserve it) parallels Christ's intercession for sinners. Nabal's hardness of heart (qashah) and his resistance to the covenant obligation to recognize David's kingship parallels humanity's resistance to Christ's kingly claim.
commentary.application: Verse 3 confronts readers with an uncomfortable mirror. It asks: What is my name becoming? Not the name on my birth certificate, but the name the community is quietly assigning me through my habitual conduct? Am I becoming known for sekhel (discernment, wisdom in navigating relationships) or for qashah (hardness, resistance to others' legitimate claims)? Am I conducting my dealings in ways that produce ma'alalim tov (good fruit, blessing) or ra ma'alalim (destructive patterns)? The verse also teaches that we can be Calebites—heirs to a covenant legacy—yet live as Nabals. Genealogy and inheritance do not secure righteousness; choices do. Finally, for those in difficult marriages or relationships, Abigail's situation is painfully recognizable: she is bound to Nabal, his folly, and his hardness. Yet the narrative will show that her wisdom, her sekhel, allows her to act with agency within constraint.
